content:
ProLogium and TDAC Announce Prospective Investments of $85 Million
Non-binding term sheets signed for approximately $85 million of investment
Existing and strategic investors investing at the business combination to participate at $10.00 per share.
Proceeds expected to support the build-out of ProLogium’s Dunkirk, France gigafactory driving it to the first 4 GW of capacity, further expansion of revenue opportunities in new markets, and other general corporate purposes.
TAIPEI, Taiwan and NEW YORK, Nov. 18, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — ProLogium Holding Inc. (“ProLogium” or the “Company”), a global leader in next-generation lithium ceramic battery technology, and Translational Development Acquisition Corp. (“TDAC”) (Nasdaq: TDAC), a special purpose acquisition company, today announced the signing of non-binding term sheets with a number of existing and strategic investors for proposed investments totaling approximately $85 million.
Under these term sheets, several existing investors in ProLogium and other strategic investors have indicated an intention to invest in connection with ProLogium’s previously announced proposed business combination with TDAC (the “Transaction). Each PIPE investment is expected to be made in common shares at $10.00 per share concurrently with the closing of the Transaction. One term sheet with a strategic partner contemplates follow-on investments after the closing of the Transaction, on terms to be agreed as part of a broader partnership plan. The proposed investments remain subject to the negotiation and execution of definitive transaction documents. ProLogium expects to use the proceeds for the build-out of its gigafactory in Dunkirk, France including unlocking further reimbursements from the $1.5bn French Government subsidy, accelerating expansion into new business applications for revenue expansion in new markets such as drones, and other general corporate purposes. The Transaction is expected to close in December 2026, subject to approval by TDAC’s shareholders and other customary closing conditions.
Vincent Yang,
Founder and Chief Executive Officer of ProLogium, said:
These term sheets reflect the interest we are seeing from investors in ProLogium’s technology and our plans to scale production of next-generation lithium ceramic batteries.
”The additional capital would help us advance construction of our Dunkirk gigafactory in France and support our continued expansion into automotive, unmanned systems, AI data centers and other application markets, serving customers in Europe and globally,”
Michael B. Hoffman,
Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of TDAC, said:
We are encouraged by the support from existing and strategic investors reflected in these term sheets.
”We are working with these investors to finalize definitive agreements as we move toward closing the Transaction,”
Advisors
Cohen & Company Capital Markets, a division of Cohen & Company Securities, LLC, is acting as the Exclusive Financial Advisor, Lead Capital Markets Advisor and Placement Agent to ProLogium. Credit Agricole Securities (USA) Inc. (and its affiliates, including Crédit Agricole Corporate and Investment Bank) is acting as a Placement Agent to ProLogium. Sullivan & Cromwell LLP and LCS & Partners are serving as legal advisors to ProLogium. BTIG, LLC, is acting as the Exclusive Financial Advisor, Lead Capital Markets Advisor and Placement Agent to TDAC. Venable is serving as legal advisor to TDAC.

Sensible Micro Named Authorized Distributor for American Lithium Energy
Partnership expands access to U.S.-manufactured lithium-ion cells, flexible stocking and scheduled releases for aerospace, defense and other demanding applications
TAMPA, Fla., Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Sensible Micro Corporation today announced an authorized distribution partnership with American Lithium Energy (ALE), expanding customer access to U.S.-manufactured cylindrical and pouch lithium-ion cells and coordinated supply planning services.
Through Sensible Micro, customers can evaluate ALE cell options, coordinate technical discussions and sourcing documentation, and develop stocking and delivery plans aligned with production needs. Sensible Micro will serve as the commercial and supply chain point of contact for purchasing, order management and scheduled releases.
Supporting Domestic Battery Sourcing
As aerospace and defense programs assess changing battery sourcing requirements, the partnership offers an additional path to evaluate domestically manufactured cells.
Section 842 of the FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act
addresses certain defense procurements involving advanced batteries and foreign entities of concern. Customers should assess applicability and compliance for their specific programs and products.
U.S. Battery Technology and Manufacturing
Founded in 2006, ALE designs and manufactures advanced lithium-ion cells and custom battery solutions for aerospace, defense, medical, mobility and energy storage applications. Its portfolio includes cylindrical and pouch cell designs, SafeCore™ safety technology and ZeroVolt™ technology, which supports repeated discharge to zero volts in applicable designs. Availability and performance depend on the selected product and application.
Flexible Distribution and Supply Planning
Sensible Micro can structure custom stocking programs and scheduled releases around agreed forecasts, order commitments and delivery requirements. These services can help customers plan availability, manage working capital and align inventory with production schedules.
Executive Perspectives
— Chris Torrioni,
Chief Executive Officer & Co-Founder, Sensible Micro Corporation, said:
Defense and aerospace customers are increasingly focused on battery sourcing, supply continuity and long-term availability.
”By pairing ALE’s U.S.-manufactured cell technologies with Sensible Micro’s stocking and distribution capabilities, we can help customers evaluate options and plan for ongoing production.”
— Dr. Jiang Fan
, Founder & President, American Lithium Energy, said:
Our partnership with Sensible Micro expands access to ALE’s U.S.-manufactured lithium-ion technologies.
”Together, we can support customers from initial cell evaluation through long-term production planning, with a focus on performance, reliability and supply chain responsiveness.”

Recycling – Charging towards the battery electric future
The Battery Innovation Programme has awarded £28.6m to 27 projects to strengthen the UK battery sector and boost national capability.
Delivered by Innovate UK on behalf of the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, the competition is designed to support UK businesses and researchers to develop new battery technologies.
The competition focused on sourcing and processing battery materials, recycling valuable materials, strengthening UK manufacturing and reducing reliance on overseas supply chains.
Recycling batteries
Lithium Battery Recyclers Ltd has been awarded more than £1.2 million to lead project Reclaim, to develop a new UK process for recycling end-of-life electric vehicle batteries.
The process, developed by the University of Leicester, uses a tiny quantity of vegetable oil in water to separate valuable battery materials, including graphite, without acid leaching or hazardous chemicals.
The project will scale up the technology at a pilot facility in Widnes, Cheshire, and test the recovered materials for reuse in new batteries.
It aims to reduce the energy needed for recycling and keep valuable battery materials in the UK to support domestic manufacturing.
Reducing waste
Hyperbat, now part of Unipart Manufacturing Group, has received more than £2.4 million to lead a project.
This aims to reduce the number of electric vehicles written off because their batteries are damaged or no longer working as expected.
At present, it can be difficult to assess whether these batteries are safe to repair or reuse.
This can lead to unnecessary vehicle write-offs, higher insurance costs and valuable materials being lost.
The project will develop a clear process for checking each battery and deciding whether it can be repaired, reused , given a second life for energy storage or safely recycled.
The work could keep batteries in use for longer, reduce waste and create skilled jobs in the UK.
Feasibility studies
The competition has also awarded just over £6.2 million to 15 shorter feasibility studies exploring new ideas across the battery supply chain.
Running for between six and 12 months, these projects will test whether early-stage technologies could improve how batteries are made, used, reused and recycled.
This will help the most promising ideas move towards further development and commercial use.
SuperDielectrics Group and Sytronix have been awarded almost £500,000 to test a new type of battery that could help data centres manage the rapid changes in electricity demand.
The water-based battery is designed to store and release power quickly, helping data centres run more AI servers without placing additional strain on local electricity networks.
The project will build on an existing battery pack and test how it responds to the changing power needs of AI systems.
If successful, the technology could help data centres make better use of their existing grid connections and expand without requiring immediate upgrades to local power supplies.
It could also provide a safer alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries and reduce reliance on imported battery materials.
Investment in skills
The Battery Innovation Programme has also awarded £3.6 million to three regional skills initiatives.
These will accelerate the development of the UK’s battery manufacturing workforce and strengthen national capability across the battery value chain.
The investment will support the delivery of industry-focused nationally accredited training programmes across England.
These will equip learners with the skills needed to secure careers in one of the UK’s fastest-growing advanced manufacturing sectors, and help businesses access talent to meet increasing demand.
University Centre Somerset will deliver Level 2 and 3 battery manufacturing training for the South West battery cluster.
University College Birmingham, and Newcastle University with New College Durham in the North East, will expand their training to Levels 4 and 5.
Dr Valentina Gentili,
Director of the Battery Innovation Programme, said:
As global demand for batteries continues to grow, it is increasingly important that the UK focuses on the areas where it can deliver the greatest impact and strategic value.
The projects supported through this competition demonstrate the breadth of innovation taking place across the UK battery sector.
Minister for
Reindustrialisation Blair McDougall,
This funding will give Britain’s battery manufacturing industry the support they need to power the industries of the future and keep our country at the cutting edge of innovation.
Through our Modern Industrial Strategy we’re doubling down on Britain’s high-growth sectors like advanced manufacturing, and I want to congratulate all the winners on their success and their role in reinforcing Britain’s leadership in this fast-growing industry.

title: Sila Inks Long-Term Offtake Deal with Panasonic Energy to Power Domestic Battery Production - Batteries News
content:
Sila Inks Long-Term Offtake Deal with Panasonic Energy to Power Domestic Battery Production
Agreement to deliver Sila’s TALAMEDA, Calif.–(
BUSINESS WIRE
, a leading battery technology and materials company, today announced a commercial offtake agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America. The multi-year agreement is part of a long-term commercial relationship with the potential for over $1 billion of offtake over time. Sila will supply its proprietary Titan Silicon® silicon-carbon (Si/C) anode material from its Moses Lake, Washington plant to power Panasonic battery cells. The partnership is also expected to support significant manufacturing and construction job creation in the United States. With Sila’s U.S.-based anode production underpinned by proprietary American technology and know-how, Panasonic and its OEM customers gain a clearer path toward a more secure, resilient, and sustainable domestic supply chain.
Gene Berdichevsky,
Co-founder and CEO of Sila, said:
This offtake agreement is a major commercial milestone for Sila, a signal that our Moses Lake plant will be ready to supply high-performance materials for our key strategic customers once qualified, and expand as needed,
“Partnering with a global industry leader like Panasonic validates our technology, ensuring anodes invented and manufactured in the U.S. are integrated into American-built cells to power critical industries for years to come.”
The agreement marks a significant step toward strengthening U.S. technological competitiveness and industrial resilience by manufacturing next-generation silicon-carbon anode materials here in the United States. Sila and Panasonic will also collaborate on intellectual property to further strengthen and develop their partnership.
Yasuaki Takamoto,
CEO, Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America, said:
Sila’s rapid progress at Moses Lake—from breaking ground to production—has been exceptional,
“Their technical leadership makes them a trusted partner as we work together toward meeting our highest quality and performance standards. This collaboration evidences Panasonic’s commitment to U.S. manufacturing while contributing to a more resilient battery supply chain in North America.”
The contract announced today follows Sila’s recent $1.4 billion loan commitment from the U.S. Department of Defense’s Office of Strategic Capital (OSC). Securing strong commercial offtake agreements represents a key milestone and a natural next step toward demonstrating Sila’s execution and commercial readiness across the business. It also results in an estimated additional 500 manufacturing and construction jobs at Sila’s plant in Moses Lake, Washington, as the company scales production to meet volume requirements for this agreement and other commercial commitments.
Sila’s Moses Lake silicon-carbon anode manufacturing facility is expected to play a pivotal role in strengthening domestic battery manufacturing and securing key energy supply chains. By scaling proprietary Titan Silicon Si/C anode production locally, the facility reinforces U.S. manufacturing leadership, fosters regional high-tech job creation, and lays the foundation of a secure, competitive battery supply chain in North America for global electric vehicle, AI, and critical technology markets.

title: Molten Industries Commissions World’s First Plant to Produce Battery-Grade Graphite - and hydrogen - from Natural Gas - Batteries News
content:
Molten Industries Commissions World’s First Plant to Produce Battery-Grade Graphite – and hydrogen – from Natural Gas
Building a domestic supply of critical materials, Molten’s Oakland demonstration plant is now operational, producing battery-grade graphite and clean hydrogen in an end-to-end, commercial-scale, modular process
OAKLAND, Calif.–(
BUSINESS WIRE
)–Molten Industries, an industrial manufacturing startup scaling a breakthrough technology to produce critical minerals and chemicals, today announced the commissioning and start of operations at its demonstration plant in Oakland, California. This milestone marks the world’s first plant to produce battery-grade graphite from natural gas, creating a new domestic source for a critical battery material and demonstrating Molten’s methane pyrolysis technology end-to-end at commercial scale.
Molten’s technology converts natural gas into two valuable products — battery-grade graphite and hydrogen — by splitting methane into its elemental components, carbon and hydrogen, without oxygen, combustion or CO₂. Compared with conventional synthetic graphite, Molten’s process uses 4× cheaper feedstock and 3× less electricity, needs no graphitization furnace, and produces zero process emissions. The process also produces clean hydrogen as a by-product, an ingredient used in global production of ammonia fertilizer, refined petroleum products, methanol, semiconductors, and steel.
Graphite is the primary material that holds charge in a lithium-ion battery, making it essential to electric vehicles, data centers, grid storage, robotics, drones, and other battery applications. Graphite is also used in nuclear reactors, semiconductor processing, jet engines, gas turbines, steelmaking, and thermal energy storage. While domestic sources of graphite for steelmaking and nuclear exist, the United States remains entirely dependent on foreign sources for battery-grade graphite, and
of global battery graphite processing is controlled by China.
Molten’s process demonstration unlocks a 100%-U.S.-made pathway for this critical material based on a widely available domestic resource, natural gas. The company’s Oakland plant has a capacity of 300 metric tons of graphite anode production per year, with reported natural gas-to-graphite yields above 95%, using a single full-scale modular reactor that serves as the building block for future plants.
Kevin Bush,
CEO and co-founder of Molten Industries, said:
Splitting natural gas into carbon and hydrogen was first patented in 1889, but nobody could figure out how to create high-quality graphite,
“We’ve created an entirely new technology to become the first to produce battery-grade graphite and hydrogen from natural gas. The Oakland plant proves that we can make these products from an abundant domestic resource in a single modular reactor — a critical step toward scaling the technology.”
Caleb Boyd,
CTO and co-founder of Molten Industries, said:
Going end to end from pipeline natural gas to battery material in a single facility at scale is modern alchemy,
“We’ve gone from a concept in the lab to an operating plant that is producing graphite and hydrogen every day and serves as the building block for larger production facilities.”

title: Addionics Reports 3.5x Cycle Life in Cylindrical Cells Tested at Avrion Battery Labs, Solving Battery Degradation While Operating Continuously at High Rate - Batteries News
content:
Addionics Reports 3.5x Cycle Life in Cylindrical Cells Tested at Avrion Battery Labs, Solving Battery Degradation While Operating Continuously at High Rate
CUPERTINO, Calif.–(
BUSINESS WIRE
)–Addionics, a developer of 3D porous current collectors for lithium-ion batteries, announced results from a case study conducted at Avrion Battery Labs showing that Addionics architecture delivered 3.5 times the cycle life and faster capacity recovery during rest, gains attributed to improved electrolyte and salt mobility inside the cell. These results demonstrate that Addionics is solving one of the biggest challenges related to battery degradation in the industry, uneven salt distribution under sustained cycling, enabling an always-on AI and autonomy industry.
The cells incorporating Addionics current collectors reached approximately 3.5 times the number of cycles before end of life, defined as 80% state of health, compared with reference cells using conventional current collectors. During rest, Addionics cells recovered in less than 2 hours initially and less than 12 hours by cycle 200, whereas reference cells required more than 48 hours after the first 20 cycles. These results are consistent with faster equilibration of electrolyte salt concentration.
Many established lithium-ion battery applications, including phones, laptops and cars, allow periods of rest or slower charging and discharging. Autonomous vehicles, humanoid robots and low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites increasingly demand sustained operation with limited opportunities for rest. In these applications, downtime can reduce availability and carry substantial operational costs.
The Avrion Labs case study demonstrates the potential of Addionics’ porous current collectors to support these demanding operating profiles by extending cycle life and reducing the time needed for recovery during rest. Avrion Labs provided the experimental platform for the study, including successful roll-to-roll electrode coating and fabrication of the graphite/NMC 18650 cylindrical cells. Testing used ultra-high precision coulometry (UHPC) equipment alongside Gamry instrumentation to track cycling performance and electrochemical impedance. Bringing cell fabrication and precision characterization together at Avrion Labs enabled Addionics to evaluate collector architecture in a practical wound-cell format.
Addionics current collectors can reduce the relaxation time of lithium diffusion by hundreds to thousands of times by reducing the diffusion distance. Any reduction in diffusion length has a squared effect on relaxation time according to a simplified diffusion model: where t is a characteristic relaxation time, L is diffusion length and D is the effective salt diffusion coefficient. The same mechanism is expected to apply whether concentration gradients form along the length of the cell or across its layers. This reduction in diffusion time is expected to be even more significant in larger format cells.
Discharge capacity and resistance relaxation results
Cells incorporating Addionics current collectors demonstrated longer cycle life and less capacity recovery after rest. These responses are consistent with reduced accumulation of reversible salt concentration gradients during cycling for cells with Addionics current collectors.
Together, the capacity and HFI responses support faster salt concentration relaxation with porous current collectors. Direct salt distribution measurements are planned to further test this mechanism.
Shortening electrolyte redistribution pathways
Sustained cycling with limited rest can leave salt unevenly distributed inside a cell due to limited electrolyte and salt ion mobility. In thick, high-loading electrodes, sustained cycling can cause concentration gradients to grow rapidly, leading to lithium plating on the anode. In addition, electrolyte motion induced salt inhomogeneity (EMSI) can develop when electrode expansion and contraction exacerbate salt concentration gradients due to the restricted movement of electrolyte. Both mechanisms are caused by kinetic limitations of electrolyte movement and salt concentration gradient relaxation. Addionics’ current collectors are designed to mitigate these limitations by reducing diffusion distance to improve the cell’s performance.
Repeated cycling can redistribute salt over centimeter-scale distances, increasing resistance and reducing accessible capacity.
(BMW AG and University of Agder) and from Jeff Dahn (Dalhousie University) with collaborators at Tesla has linked EMSI to capacity loss and localized lithium plating in large-format and silicon-containing cells. [1, 2] Conventional solid metal foil current collectors block direct electrolyte transport across the current collector, leaving longer pathways for redistribution within the jelly roll. Addionics’ porous architecture introduces through-plane pathways through the current collector, allowing electrolyte and salt to redistribute across electrode layers. The engineering objective is to shorten the distance over which concentration gradients must relax. Addionics and Avrion plan follow-up work to confirm this, with the mechanism findings to be shared in a technical note.
Implications for battery engineering
The results support further development of current collector architecture as a way to manage internal electrolyte transport. This approach is relevant to applications with repeated cycling and limited rest, including robotics and autonomous fleets. It also motivates testing under other transport-limited conditions, such as low temperatures, larger cell formats and thicker electrodes. At Avrion Labs, Addionics tested performance in 18650s down to -10 °C, where improved performance at high rates and low temperatures were observed.
Cell design and test conditions
Two groups of 18650 cylindrical cells were fabricated using NMC811 cathodes and graphite anodes: a control group with conventional current collectors and a group incorporating Addionics 3D porous current collectors. The cells were evaluated under the following conditions.
The Business Use Case
For autonomous taxis and electric fleets, battery performance directly affects vehicle cost and revenue-generating uptime. Addionics’ illustrative model shows that expanding the usable battery window from 60% to 80% could deliver a third more usable energy, or meet the same energy requirement with approximately 25% less battery capacity. Assuming $50,000 vehicles with batteries representing 35% of cost, the smaller packs could save about $4.4 million across 1,000 autonomous taxis. In a separate space example, extending a $5 million satellite’s operating life from five to six years would add a productive year without another build or launch, improving the return on an asset already in orbit.

title: The Volkswagen ID. Buzz Beach is an electric van built for camping, but it's not cheap
content:
Volkswagen
ID. Buzz
Peter Johnson
| Nov 19 2026 - 7:51 am PT
Volkswagen introduced the
ID. Buzz Beach,
a fun spin on its electric van that’s built for camping and overnight stays. However, it won’t be cheap, starting at over $70,000.
Meet the Volkswagen ID. Buzz Beach
Volkswagen’s original microbus became a cultural icon thanks to its open, customizable interior, making it perfect for large families, road trips, camping, and, of course, music festivals.
The ID. Buzz brings the classic Type 2 microbus into the electric era with a retro-new style, modern tech, and a flexible, spacious cabin.
Building on its reputation as a symbol of freedom and adventure, Volkswagen is adding a new member to the electric people mover lineup.
The new ID. Buzz Beach “brings adventure into the electric age,” Volkswagen said after introducing the new variant on Thursday. Designed for camping, longer road trips, and overnight stays, the electric van will be available in 5-, 6-, and 7-seat configurations.
Volkswagen said it sleeps two comfortably with a removable bed frame and a custom-fitting folding mattress.
Volkswagen ID. Buzz Beach fold-out mattress (Source: VW UK)
The mattress is a decent size at about 6.5 feet long by 4 feet wide (2.0m x 1.2m), roughly the size of an average small double bed.
In the 5-seat configuration, the bed frame tucks away in the trunk, while in the 6- and 7-seat layouts, it’s stored vertically behind the third row of seats.
For camping and other longer stays, Volkswagen added a new Overnight mode that uses the vehicle’s battery to provide up to 48 hours of continuous, off-grid climate control. The new mode can be accessed on the center touchscreen.
It also includes blackout curtains throughout the cabin and ventilation grilles on the front side windows.
The ID. Buzz Beach offers vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities. A 230V power socket adaptor comes standard, letting you power an e-bike, charge a smartphone, run camping equipment, or power other external electronic devices. A camping connector is available as an added option.
To top it off, Volkswagen added a hidden foldable table and chairs set that can be tucked away without taking up internal space.
Volkswagen will open orders for the new ID. Buzz Beach in the UK later this month, starting at £53,955 (excluding VAT), or about $71,000. Including VAT and OTR costs, it will start at £65,837, or roughly $86,500.
What about those in the US? VW introduced the 2027 ID. Buzz with
a new Tourer model
that was essentially the same as the Beach variant in the UK, with a fold-out mattress, Overnight mode, blackout curtains, and a table and chairs set.
However, VW told its US dealers in September that it would be
delaying the ID. Buzz’s return
until the 2028 model year.
The 2025 Volkswagen ID. Buzz started at about $60,000 in the US, which is one of the biggest reasons it failed to catch on with buyers. The original VW microbus was an affordable people mover.
A custom camper variant would likely cost more than $70,000. Would you pay $70,000 or more for Volkswagen’s electric camper van?

title: Aptera (SEV) completes its first customer solar EV — for its top crowdfunder
content:
Aptera (SEV) has finished building its first solar electric vehicle for a paying customer. It’s going to Martin Hartono, the startup’s No. 1 “Accelerator” investor, and it’s being exported out of the US.
It’s a real milestone for a company that has pushed back its delivery dates since 2022. And it comes a week after Aptera reported $9.2 million in cash against the roughly $25 million it says it needs to start series production.
A matte black Aptera for Accelerator #1
Aptera announced today from its Carlsbad, California headquarters that it completed what it calls its first production solar electric vehicle. The car is finished in “Noir,” a matte black exterior, and was built for Accelerator #1.
Accelerators are investors from Aptera’s community funding program, where delivery priority goes to whoever invests the most. So the first customer car went to the biggest check.
Hartono is the CEO of GDP Venture, the Jakarta-based venture arm of Indonesia’s Djarum Group. Aptera didn’t say which country the car is going to, what he paid for it, or when it will actually be handed over.
In the release, Hartono said Aptera is a fit for people who want to “minimize their energy consumption without compromising the ability to travel long distances.” Co-CEO Chris Anthony called it “the moment our team has worked toward for years” and said the company is working to finish more vehicles for early customers as soon as possible.
No number was given for how many more.
Where Aptera actually stands
The timing is interesting. Just seven weeks ago, Aptera cut its estimated cost to start production to about $25 million, down from $40 to $45 million, and said the first 40 production vehicles would start building by the end of 2026, with customer deliveries in early 2027 “subject to financing.”
Its Q3 report last week didn’t change that picture much. Aptera ended September with $9.2 million in cash, and $4.1 million of that is refundable reservation fees. It lost $14 million in the quarter, and its own filing says substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern “has not been alleviated.”
On November 10, it priced a $6 million registered direct offering at $1.75 per share. SEV closed at $1.67 on Tuesday, with a 52-week high of $7.
The solar side of the pitch holds up better. In August, TÜV Rheinland measured 4.23 to 4.75 kWh per day going into the battery from the car’s integrated panels in Carlsbad, which works out to roughly 40 miles of daily driving. But that conversion relies on Aptera’s 100 Wh/mile efficiency target, and today’s release itself notes that figure isn’t yet confirmed for production vehicles.
The release’s risk factors are also worth reading. They list export, import, certification and registration requirements, state dealer licensing, single-source suppliers, and whether reservations will convert into binding orders. Shipping car No. 1 to an investor overseas sidesteps most of those for now.
Electrek’s Take
Credit where it’s due. Aptera has a finished car built to a customer’s spec, which is more than Lightyear or Sono Motors ever got to before they ran out of money. We’ve followed this company since it came back in 2019, and plenty of people (us included, at times) didn’t think we’d see this day.
Top comment by GreenBoomerang
A positive achievement, but the question remains: Is this essentially a hand-built prototype and a token delivery to one very rich customer, or is it the first of many more vehicles that will roll off an assembly line for regular people over the next couple months?
But I have to be honest, this looks more symbolic than like the start of a production ramp. This is a single vehicle, built before Aptera has raised the money it says it needs for series production, and it went to the person who put the most money into the company. That’s a thank-you and a good press release ahead of what will likely be another raise. It doesn’t tell us much about Aptera’s ability to build cars at a cost that works.
The real test is still the first 40 cars, and whether they reach regular reservation holders in the US. Aptera says it needs about $25 million to get there. It has $9.2 million, $4.1 million of which customers can ask back for, and it’s raising money at under $2 a share, which means a lot of dilution for every dollar.
We want this to work. Ultra-efficient cars are the only way vehicle-integrated solar makes sense, and Aptera is the last serious attempt standing. So can it fund those 40 cars before the cash runs out?

title: Elon Musk announces another Tesla vehicle no one asked for
content:
Elon Musk says Tesla plans to build a version of the Model Y with no steering wheel and no pedals, a driverless people-mover he describes as “good for transporting groups of 6 or 7 people.”
It’s yet another vehicle nobody asked for, from a company that ended Model S and Model X production this year and is about to end the Cybertruck. And the data says very few car buyers want a car they can’t drive.
What Musk said
Musk made the comments on stage at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday.
He pitched it as the answer to the Cybercab only carrying two people. “We still need autonomous vehicles if you’ve got 4 or 6, or a whole family,” Musk said, before adding that Tesla plans “an autonomous version of the Model Y that won’t have steering wheels or pedals.”
There was no timeline, no price and no word on where it would be built.
Six or seven seats points straight at the Model Y L, the stretched three-row Model Y that Tesla launched in the US in July for $61,990, or the regular Model Y with the $2,500 seven-seat option Tesla brought back in January.
The Model Y L wasn’t supposed to need to exist
Here’s the funny part. When Tesla launched the Model Y L in China in August 2025, Musk said it might never come to the US, “given the advent of self-driving in America.”
The idea was that autonomy would make a bigger family car pointless. Less than a year later, Tesla was building the Model Y L at Giga Texas and selling it at the top of the Model Y lineup.
Now Musk wants a driverless version of that same car. So families still need a big vehicle, self-driving or not. That’s what we said in 2025.
Tesla’s Model Y robotaxis already have a steering wheel
The robotaxi argument doesn’t hold up either. Tesla’s Robotaxi fleet is mostly Model Ys, and those cars have a steering wheel and pedals.
The wheel isn’t what’s stopping them from driving themselves. Removing it mostly makes the car useless outside Tesla’s geofences.
We’ve already seen what that looks like. Tesla opened personal Cybercab orders last week at $29,990, but the car only works inside Robotaxi service areas and requires a $299 per month subscription to operate at all.
There’s also the regulatory mess. Tesla self-certified the Cybercab as compliant with federal safety standards even though FMVSS 135 calls for a foot-operated service brake, and NHTSA responded with a Special Order in September. Zoox took the slower route and got a Part 555 exemption, which caps it at 2,500 vehicles a year. A second vehicle with no controls means a second round of that fight.
Buyers don’t want cars without controls
Cox Automotive’s 2026 Autonomous Vehicle Study asked US consumers which level of autonomy they’d find most appealing in a vehicle they own. Only 10% picked fully driverless Level 5, down from 17% when Cox first asked in 2016.
The most popular choice was Level 4 at 28%: full autonomy, but with the option for a human to drive. And only 38% said they’d feel safe in a Level 5 vehicle, compared to 87% for a modern car with basic driver aids.
So after a decade of exposure to self-driving tech, interest in a car with no controls went down, not up.
Electrek’s Take
Tesla already makes the Model Y. It already makes a six-seat Model Y. Just make the Model Y.
In 2016, Musk’s Master Plan Part Deux promised to “expand the electric vehicle product line to address all major segments.” Ten years later, once the Cybertruck ends next summer, Tesla’s consumer lineup is the Model 3 and Model Y. That’s it. No affordable car (Musk called a non-robotaxi $25,000 Tesla “pointless” in 2024), no compact crossover, no minivan, no midsize pickup.
Top comment by Doug T
Teslafsdtracker is the only real source of Tesla ADS/ADAS capability.
It shows a safety critical intervention is needed every 2000 miles. That is less than 1% of whats needed to remove a human from the real time loop. Hence Tesla's hiding of intervention data and operational parameters, and the control centers where humans watch real time video feeds and initiate interventions when needed.
Tesla L4 is all smoke and mirrors. All they have is a L2 system driving in geo restricted zones with driver oversight shifted from the front seat to a control center
Every time there’s a gap in Tesla’s lineup, Musk gives the same answer: autonomy will fill it. The Model Y L was going to be unnecessary. The cheap car was pointless. The Model S and X made way for Optimus, and the Cybertruck for the Cybercab.
But Tesla’s own robotaxi fleet proves you don’t need to remove the steering wheel to run a robotaxi. Keeping it costs Tesla almost nothing and keeps the car useful for the roughly 90% of buyers who still want the option to drive. Taking it out only adds a federal compliance fight and shrinks the market to people who live inside a geofence.
If Tesla wants to sell more cars, it should build cars people are asking for. Who exactly is asking for this one?

title: Porsche’s newest electric car is a tiny 50 mph replica of a legendary racer
content:
Micah Toll
| Nov 19 2026 - 3:36 am PT
Porsche’s latest electric vehicle isn’t a new Taycan or Macan EV. In fact, it’s not even a full-sized car. Instead, the German automaker has teamed up with British luxury miniature car builder Hedley Studios to create an 80%-scale electric replica of one of Porsche’s most iconic racing cars, the legendary 550 Spyder.
Known as the Porsche 550 J, the pint-sized electric sports car will make its public debut at the Icons of Porsche festival in Dubai on November 21-22, celebrating 75 years of Porsche motorsport.
Hedley Studios
sounds familiar, that’s because we’ve covered the company before, back when it was known as The Little Car Company. Among its more entertaining projects was
a life-sized recreation of the famous Japanese Tamiya Wild One RC dune buggy
, turning a childhood remote-controlled favorite into an actual drivable electric vehicle. We’ve also covered the company’s ultra-luxurious miniature electric cars, including its
stunning Bentley Blower recreation
Now the company has turned its attention to Porsche, and the result is perhaps its most impressive miniature EV yet.
There’s something I love about miniature electric cars, combining the fun of four-wheels with the right-sized (or pint-sized) magic of mini-mobility.
The Porsche 550 J is based on the original 550 Spyder, Porsche’s first purpose-built racing sports car, which debuted in 1953 and went on to become a motorsport legend.
Despite being scaled down to 80% of the original’s dimensions, the new electric version still seats two adults. It weighs just 350 kg (772 lb), thanks partly to its lightweight tubular steel spaceframe and hand-formed carbon fiber bodywork.
The standard version features an 8 kW (11 hp) electric motor operating on a 48V system, providing a top speed of 40 mph (65 km/h) and a range of up to 30 miles (50 km).
For those who want a bit more performance from their miniature Porsche, an optional RS Pack doubles the power to 16 kW (21 hp), increases the top speed to 50 mph (80 km/h), and extends the range to 50 miles (80 km) thanks to additional batteries. The upgrade also includes drilled disc brakes and adjustable suspension.
The attention to detail goes well beyond the exterior. The car features Brembo brakes, Bilstein suspension, Continental tires, and even a wood-rimmed Nardi steering wheel, just like the original. The classic dashboard retains its three-dial layout, though the fuel gauge has been replaced with a battery meter and the original choke lever now serves as a drive mode selector.
Even the charging port is cleverly hidden beneath the chrome fuel filler cap.
The project was developed in close collaboration with Porsche over six years, with Hedley Studios gaining access to original engineering drawings, archival materials, and historic vehicles in Porsche’s museum.
Only 250 examples will be produced, with buyers able to choose historic racing liveries or custom paint finishes, including colors matching their full-sized Porsches.
Of course, this level of craftsmanship doesn’t come cheap.
Prices start at £69,500
(approximately US $91,000), before taxes and options. Orders are already open through Porsche dealers and Hedley Studios, with deliveries expected to begin in spring 2027.
That’s a lot of money for a car that’s only 80% there, but then again, this isn’t really meant to be practical transportation. It’s a collector’s piece that just happens to be electric, drivable, and capable of hitting 50 mph. When there are only 250 of these being built, the £70k price is really just the entry ticket to a special, ultra-luxury club of electric mini-Porsches.
And if you ask me, that sounds like a pretty fun combination. I don’t think I’ll ever be in the market for one of these personally, but I’d sure love to be friends with someone who is!

title: SolarEdge debuts dual-module power optimizer - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Duo cuts the number of optimizers needed in half, works with dual-tilt racking and with Arc Fault Detection, every optimizer becomes an arc sensor.
Anne Fischer
19 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Inverters
SolarEdge unveiled its new U.S.-made Duo power optimizer for commercial and industrial (C&I) solar projects this week at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas.
Power optimizers are DC-to-DC converters installed on the underside of solar modules to maximize power output. Unlike conventional optimizers, which typically connect to a single module, the SolarEdge Duo connects to two modules, with an independent maximum power point tracker (MPPT) for each.
According to the company’s datasheet, each input supports up to 650 W, with an MPPT operating voltage range of 12.5 V to 57 V and a maximum continuous input current of 20 A. The optimizer has a maximum output voltage of 80 V, a maximum output current of 20 A and a weighted efficiency of 98.8%.
SolarEdge said the dual-module design reduces the number of optimizers required by 50% compared with its C651U model. Each optimizer features a short pair of wires for the nearest module and a pre-extended pair for the adjacent module, reducing cable slack and eliminating the need for field-installed jumpers. The Duo also supports dual-tilt racking configurations, allowing it to connect modules facing different directions.
The device measures 129 mm x 159 mm x 59 mm and weighs 1.2 kg, including cables. It has an IP68/NEMA 6P protection rating and an operating temperature range of -40 C to 85 C, with power derating above 65 C. The optimizer supports a maximum system voltage of 1,000 V and is compatible with specified SolarEdge commercial three-phase inverters.
The Duo features SolarEdge’s optimizer-level arc fault detection technology, which uses each optimizer as an arc sensor as part of the company’s arc fault circuit interruption (AFCI) system. According to SolarEdge, this enables arc faults to be detected closer to their source rather than solely at the inverter. If one optimizer fails to detect an arc, a neighboring optimizer can detect it, the company said. The system reportedly provides protection for strings with a total cable length of up to 1,000 meters between the inverter and optimizers.
SolarEdge reports that its Sense Connect technology also monitors temperature at every input and output connector to identify developing faults.
The Duo comes with a 25-year warranty. Manufactured in Florida, it is designed to meet U.S. Domestic Content and Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements.
The Duo power optimizer is available to order now in the U.S. through SolarEdge sales channels and distribution partners, with shipments expected to begin in January 2027. SolarEdge is showing the Duo this week at RE+ in booth N1516.

title: MicroQuanta, Zhejiang University achieve world-record efficiency of 23.9% for 19.48 cm² perovskite solar module - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
The result was certified by the National PV Industry Measurement and Testing Center (NPVM) of China’s Fujian Metrology Institute.
Lior Kahana
19 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Perovskite mini-module (left) and lab cell (right).
A research team led by scientists from Chinese perovskite solar cell manufacturer
MicroQuanta Semiconductor
has achieved a certified steady-state efficiency of 23.9% for a 19.48 cm² perovskite mini-module, setting a new world record.
The researchers said the result was enabled by cooling the wet perovskite precursor film before vacuum treatment to slow crystallization and reduce the fill factor losses associated with scaling up from cells to modules.
“What makes our result special is that the world record is achieved at the module level, rather than in a small laboratory cell,” corresponding author Dongchen Lan told
pv magazine
. “Solar cells often lose efficiency when scaled up into modules.”
The result was certified by the
National PV Industry Measurement and Testing Center
(NPVM) of China’s
Fujian Metrology Institute
Lan said the team identified a major cause of these losses and demonstrated a way to mitigate them while helping modules maintain their performance over time. “This addresses a key challenge in bringing next-generation solar technologies closer to practical use,” he said.
The researchers first compared laboratory-scale perovskite solar cells with mini-modules fabricated under matched processing conditions in previous studies. They used Shapley value analysis, which averages the contribution of each parameter across all possible orders of substitution, to quantify the contributions of open-circuit voltage, short-circuit current density, and fill factor to the measured efficiency loss.
After accounting for current losses in inactive areas created by laser scribing, they found that fill factor was the largest contributor to the efficiency drop from cells to modules.
Cell performance with and without precursor cooling
To reduce that loss, the team spin-coated a perovskite precursor onto indium tin oxide (ITO)-coated glass carrying two hole-transport layers (HTLs). Immediately after coating, they cooled the wet film for 15 seconds to 0-10 C, transferred it to a vacuum chamber within about five seconds, and vacuum-flashed it for two minutes before annealing it at 110 C for 30 minutes. They then applied a surface passivation layer and deposited the electron-transport layers (ETLs) and silver (Ag) electrode. Measurements during film formation showed that cooling slowed the conversion of an intermediate phase into perovskite, yielding films with larger, more uniform grains.
The researchers used slot-die coating to fabricate a 19.48 cm² perovskite mini-module consisting of eight subcells connected in series through laser scribing. The device was built on a glass substrate coated with indium tin oxide (ITO), nickel oxide (NiOₓ), and a self-assembled monolayer known as 3PATAT-C3. It featured a formamidinium-cesium lead iodide (FA₀.₉₅Cs₀.₀₅PbI₃) absorber with an ethylenediammonium diiodide (EDAI₂) surface passivation layer, a fullerene (C₆₀) electron transport layer, a bathocuproine (BCP) buffer layer, and a silver (Ag) electrode.
According to the team’s measurements, the mini-module achieved a certified steady-state efficiency of 23.9% and a fill factor of 83.3%, which the authors reported as the highest for a perovskite module. It also had a geometric fill factor of 97%, meaning 97% of its aperture area was photoactive. In separate aging tests under continuous one-sun illumination at open-circuit, the efficiency loss attributable to declining fill factor was less than one-third as large in modules made with the cooling step as in control modules.
“The resulting fill factor advantage is retained across device scales and during operation, revealing a shared parameter-level pattern between scale-up loss and operational decay,” the group concluded. “Hence, preserving fill factor offers a unifying optimization target for developing efficient, stable and scalable perovskite photovoltaics.”
The cell was described in the study “
Retarding efficiency loss upon scaling in perovskite photovoltaics as fill factor becomes the bottleneck
,” published in
nature communications.
Researchers from China’s
MicroQuanta Semiconductor
Zhejiang University,
China Three Gorges Renewable
Zhejiang Provincial Key Laboratory of Optoelectronic Functional Materials and Devices
, and the
Australian Centre for Advanced Photovoltaics
In January 2025, MicroQuanta
achieved a certified efficiency of 21.86%
for an 810 cm² perovskite solar module. The company has also been developing a gigawatt-scale perovskite production line in Quzhou, Zhejiang province, with plans to manufacture large-area modules measuring 2.88 m² and targeting 20% efficiency and a 25-year lifespan.
More recently, MicroQuanta
introduced a perovskite-silicon tandem module
for building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) at The smarter E Europe 2026 in Munich, Germany. The four-terminal MQ-α² series features a reported efficiency of 26% and power outputs ranging from 65 W to 165 W. The modules are available in customizable colors and finishes.

title: Solyco unveils 485 W full-black residential solar module with stainless steel protection - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The German manufacturer’s new glass-glass solar panel features back-contact cells, a power conversion efficiency of 23.8% and a bifaciality factor of approximately 70%. It comes with a 30-year product warranty and an 88.85% power output guarantee after 30 years.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
19 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Residential
Solyco adds stainless steel cable protection to its 485 W solar module
German solar module manufacturer Solyco has introduced a new full-black, glass-glass solar module for residential applications.
The Solyco Design R-BG 108nBC.6 Protect panel features a stainless steel cover for its connection cables, designed to protect them against mechanical damage, animal bites and ultraviolet (UV) radiation.
The module features 108 monocrystalline half-cut cells based on back-contact (BC) technology, delivering a power output of 485 W and a conversion efficiency of 23.8%. Under standard test conditions (STC), it has a maximum power voltage of 33.94 V and a maximum power current of 14.30 A. Its open-circuit voltage is 40.89 V, while its short-circuit current is 15.03 A.
The back-contact cell design places electrical connections on the rear of the cells, reducing front-side shading and providing a full-black appearance. The module has a bifaciality factor of around 70%. It features three separate junction boxes, each equipped with a bypass diode, with an IP68 protection rating. The 4 mm² solar cables are 1.2 m long and fitted with Stäubli MC4-Evo 2 connectors.
The module measures 1,800 mm × 1,134 mm × 30 mm and weighs 24.8 kg. It features 2 mm tempered solar glass on both sides and a black-anodized aluminum frame.
The operating temperature ranges from -40 C to 85 C, with a nominal module operating temperature (NMOT) of 42 C. The temperature coefficient is -0.26%/C.
The module supports a maximum system voltage of 1,500 V and a maximum reverse current of 30 A. It can withstand front-side loads of up to 5,400 Pa and rear-side loads of up to 2,400 Pa. The manufacturer also claims resistance to hailstones measuring up to 30 mm in diameter at impact speeds of 23.9 m/s.
Solyco offers a product warranty of up to 30 years and guarantees 88.85% of the module’s initial power output after 30 years.
According to the manufacturer, the R-BG 108nBC.6 Protect is its first commercially available module featuring integrated protection against animal bites for its connection cables.
Berlin-based Solyco Solar has expanded its portfolio of high-efficiency PV modules and specialized solar technologies in recent years. In July 2026, the company
introduced a 500 W full-black back-contact module
with an efficiency of 24.5%, following the
launch of a 480 W back-contact panel
in August 2025. The company has also developed
a low-temperature solar cell interconnection technology
designed to reduce material costs and
vertical PV systems for green rooftops

title: Jackery and Every Electric launch 4 MWh plug-in battery VPP for New York renters - pv magazine Global
content: Portable power station manufacturer Jackery and consumer energy aggregator Every Electric have partnered to roll out what they call North America’s first plug-in battery aimed at renters and apartment residents. By aggregating behind-the-meter storage, the setup uses standard wall outlets rather than hardwired residential systems that require electricians. The tie-up is part of an Every Electric program that has operated across Consolidated Edison’s New York City service territory since September. Roughly 2,000 portable power stations, mostly Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 , are currently distributed across more than 1,000 households, providing 4 MWh of flexible storage capacity. According to the companies, nearly 50 MWh of energy has cycled through the units to date. The companies are calling it the “continent’s first plug-and-play virtual power plant (VPP) distribution network based on self-contained, expandable portable power stations”. Onboarding requires residents to register online, link their utility account, and plug a window or portable air conditioner into the drop-shipped battery’s passthrough outlet. Once connected to Wi-Fi via Jackery’s app, Every Electric’s cloud software automates charging during off-peak hours and discharges the battery to run the air conditioner during peak grid demand, while keeping backup capacity available for outages. The setup is similar to how plug-in storage has worked in Europe’s balcony solar market, and requires no electrician labor, municipal permits, or other agreements. How it works Every Electric offers options, both tied to a portable battery and an air conditioning unit. In the first option, the cost to the household is nothing upfront for the hardware, setup, or a monthly fee, and a refundable security deposit is $30. As part of the deal, Every Electric retains ownership of the battery, collects demand-response revenue through Con Edison’s Smart Usage program, and pays residents $100 to $150 per year per air conditioner. In the second option, a separate ownership tier lets households buy a unit outright for $650, discounted from a $999 list price, to raise annual payouts to up to $250 per air conditioner while cross-subsidizing a free unit for a neighbor, alongside a zero-deposit waitlisted option for next summer. A third option appears to be accepting a BYO battery as well, and Every Electric has details of operating with other brands outside of Jackery, with photos showing EcoFlow and Bluetti portable power stations. Total seasonal payouts across participating New York homes are approaching $200,000. Every Electric reports a waitlist of more than 15,000 air conditioners looking to join the network. “Traditional solar and storage require a roof, a garage or a permanent professional installation, which leaves renters and multifamily residents out,” said Andrew Wang, co-founder and CEO of Every Electric. “With Every Electric, adding grid services capabilities lets any household with a wall outlet earn on their bills while supporting the broader electrical infrastructure.” Both companies are demonstrating the platform at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas from November 17 to 19, where Jackery is also exhibiting its modular Explorer 5000 Plus system with smart transfer switch support. title: Tesla seeks Texas tax break for $3.1 billion polysilicon plant - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Tesla says it will build a polysilicon plant in Texas only if the state cuts its property tax bill, as it seeks to produce solar’s most China-dominated material at home.
Brian Publicover
19 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Manufacturing
polysilicon
US electric vehicle and clean energy company Tesla has applied for a Texas property tax limitation for a proposed $3.1 billion polysilicon refinery near Robstown, Nueces County, saying it would not build the plant in the state without the incentive.
The application, filed with the Tuloso-Midway Independent School District under the state’s Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation (JETI) program, has been published by the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts.
Tesla describes the plant as “under consideration for development” and as the “upstream component of Tesla’s vertically integrated domestic solar manufacturing platform.” It says that “in the absence of the agreement the applicant would not make the proposed investment in this state” and that it is assessing locations in other jurisdictions.
The plant would produce ultra-high-purity polysilicon for single-crystal silicon ingots and N-type, high-efficiency solar cells. Its equipment list includes a hydrochlorination and trichlorosilane synthesis unit, chlorosilane distillation and purification trains, silicon tetrachloride recycling loops and Siemens chemical vapor deposition reactors. The filing does not state the plant’s production capacity.
Investment timeline
An economic impact analysis prepared for Tesla by EY puts construction between 2027 and 2030. Of the planned capital spending, $1.5 billion is earmarked for engineering and construction, $1.4 billion for equipment and $183 million for utility infrastructure, with more than 80% spent in 2028 and 2029.
Tesla plans to hire 260 workers in 2030, rising to 515 once the plant is fully operational in 2032, at average total compensation of $130,000, according to the analysis. Construction would support an average of 550 direct jobs a year. EY estimates the project would generate about $63.5 billion in economic output in Texas through 2065.
Tesla said in the filing that more than 90% of the world’s solar-grade polysilicon is produced in China.
Under the schedule in the EY analysis, the project’s taxable value for school-district maintenance and operations taxes would be cut to zero from 2028 to 2030 and halved from 2031 through 2040. The Comptroller must review the application, and both the Office of the Governor and the school district’s board must approve an agreement before it takes effect.
The application follows Tesla’s
JETI filing for Project Crystal Sun
, a proposed solar cell and module factory in Fort Bend County, Texas, with planned investment of about $10.1 billion. That project
cleared a key tax hurdle in September
when the local school board backed its limitation.
The US government’s
Section 232 tariffs and minimum import prices on polysilicon
, which also impose a 15% duty on imported ingots, wafers, cells and modules, take effect on Dec. 4. The
minimum import prices are designed to force foreign suppliers to match US production costs
, raising the value of domestic feedstock in a market where
US polysilicon production remains limited
. Solar manufacturer Toyo
secured US polysilicon supply to navigate trade barriers
in January.
Tesla has been
advancing a plan to build 100 GW of US PV manufacturing capacity by 2028
, a target that has drawn
scrutiny over whether Elon Musk’s solar ambitions are achievable
. The company has taken a similar approach in storage, where it said in 2025 that its
10 GWh lithium iron phosphate cell factory in Nevada was nearing completion
as it reduced reliance on imported cells.

Applications & Installations

The 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) ran from 9 to 20 November 2026. On 11 November, at the side event “Clean Energy Systems: From NDCs to Implementation” – hosted by the Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization (GEIDCO) at the UNFCCC Capacity Building Hub – Floria Wang, Head of Global Branding at LONGi, delivered a keynote speech in which she shared the company’s practical achievements in advancing the global energy transition.
During her remarks, Wang introduced LONGi’s implementation practices across four dimensions.
Empowering industrial transformation and promoting low-carbon, intelligent upgrading across the industrial sector.
For diverse industrial fields such as manufacturing, construction, and logistics, LONGi provides customized photovoltaic and energy storage solutions that help enterprises replace traditional fossil fuels with clean electricity, effectively reducing operating costs and carbon footprints while enabling low-carbon and intelligent industrial transformation and upgrading.
Empowering rural and agricultural development to unlock sustainable economic vitality in rural areas.
LONGi actively promotes the “energy + rural revitalization” development model in many developing regions. For example, since 2024, Shaanxi Province has been rolling out the “PV+” rural revitalization demonstration project, under which the government provides overall coordination; village collectives establish village-owned new energy companies as the investment and loan entities; and farming households only provide rooftop space and bear no investment or loan risk. LONGi is responsible for the construction, operation, and maintenance of the power stations, while State Grid Shaanxi is responsible for grid capacity expansion and upgrading. Banks provide long-term green inclusive loans with an 18-year term. Power generation revenue is first used to repay loan principal and interest; after deducting loan repayments and operation and maintenance costs, net revenue is distributed between the village company and villagers at a ratio of 2:8. In addition, the project offers the option of installing air-source heat pumps, with dividend income from power generation covering heating expenses, allowing villagers to enjoy clean winter heating free of charge.
Empowering low-carbon urban development and building distributed clean energy systems for cities.
Empowering remote areas and vulnerable communities to close the global energy poverty gap.

title: Bolivia launches EPC tender for 40 MWac solar project - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Bolivia’s state-owned utility ENDE is seeking an EPC contractor for a project scheduled for completion in June 2028. The solar plant will be financed in part by a loan from German development bank KfW.
Luis Ini
19 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Americas
Utility-scale
The Uyuni PV plant in Bolivia
Bolivia’s state-owned power utility ENDE has launched an international tender for the engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) of the Contorno Bajo I solar plant, which will have a minimum nominal capacity of 40 MWac. The project will become the first large-scale solar power plant in the department of La Paz.
The tender, published on Nov. 16 under reference ENDE-KFW-2026-002, sets a 14-month implementation period from the signing of the contract. Construction is scheduled to begin in May 2027, with commissioning expected to be completed by June 2028.
The contract includes a 24.9/115 kV step-up substation, an approximately 800-meter-long, 115 kV interconnection line, and modifications to a bay at the Contorno Bajo substation, owned by ENDE Transmisión, to feed electricity into Bolivia’s National Interconnected System (SIN).
Bidders must demonstrate experience in five PV projects of at least 40 MW each and three solar power plants in South America that have been operational for at least two years. They must also demonstrate average annual revenue of at least €60 million ($65.93 million) and access to financial resources totaling €40 million ($43.96 million).
A separate tender for consulting and project supervision services is also underway, with bids due by Dec. 21. The contract covers construction supervision, equipment quality control, plant commissioning and training for ENDE personnel.
pv magazine Latam
reported in June
, the Bolivian government enacted legislation approving a loan of up to €34 million ($37.36 million) from German development bank KfW to finance the project.
According to information released by ENDE in July, the solar plant will occupy 34 hectares at an altitude of more than 3,700 meters above sea level and will have an estimated operational lifetime of 25 years.
original project design, announced in January 2023
, included a lithium-ion battery energy storage system. However, the current tender notice makes no mention of a storage component.

title: France’s first canal-top PV project goes online - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The 299 kW installation is expected to generate 404 MWh annually. Société du Canal de Provence estimates that its canal network could accommodate more than 50 MW of solar capacity, with potential annual generation of 70 GWh.
Gwénaëlle Deboutte,
François Puthod
19 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Highlights
Utility-scale
With an installed capacity of 299 kW, the solar canopy generates approximately 404 MWh per year.
The Provence-Alpes-Côte d’Azur regional government and Société du Canal de Provence (SCP) have completed what they describe as France’s first large-scale canal-top PV project in Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume, in the Var department.
Spanning 71 meters, the custom-designed installation covers the canal and its banks, demonstrating a new approach that combines water transport and electricity generation on the same infrastructure. With an installed capacity of 299 kW and estimated annual generation of 404 MWh, the pilot project accounts for approximately 1% of SCP’s annual energy consumption.
SCP has a long history in hydropower and currently operates 17 small hydroelectric plants, generating approximately 17 GWh per year. The company plans to expand this capacity in the coming years.
More than 50 MW of solar potential along canals
SCP aims to become a net energy producer, eventually generating more renewable electricity than its estimated annual consumption of 40 GWh. Since the early 2020s, the company has been adding solar PV to its existing hydropower portfolio.
Developed under the regional concession for the Canal de Provence, the pilot project also aims to help control water service costs. It makes use of existing infrastructure without requiring additional land development, while potentially improving water quality through the shading provided by the solar panels.
With nearly 70 km of open-air canals, the Canal de Provence, part of the Provence-Alpes-Côte d’Azur region’s hydraulic infrastructure, offers significant potential for solar PV development. SCP studies estimate that the canals could accommodate more than 50 MW of PV capacity, generating approximately 70 GWh of electricity annually.
However, deployment will be selective, with only 5% to 10% of the canal network considered suitable for PV installations due to technical and regulatory constraints.

content:

The initiative aims to strengthen Europe’s solar manufacturing industry by supporting high-efficiency solar cells, advanced production equipment, automated manufacturing processes and industrial-scale pilot production lines.
Emiliano Bellini
19 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Cell coating on a Meyer Burger demonstration line
The European Commission is preparing to launch a €36 million ($39.5 million) funding call under the Horizon Europe program to support the development and industrial scale-up of advanced solar photovoltaic manufacturing technologies.
Production technologies for solar photovoltaics beyond the state-of-the-art
call is part of the European Partnership for Innovation in Photovoltaics (EUPI-PV). It aims to strengthen Europe’s competitiveness in solar manufacturing and support the development of more efficient, reliable and cost-effective solar cells and modules.
The call is scheduled to open on Dec. 3, 2026, with an application deadline of March 31, 2027.
The funding will target advanced manufacturing processes for high-efficiency PV technologies, including production equipment, automation, digitalization and scalable industrial manufacturing methods. Projects must demonstrate improvements over commercially available technologies while addressing production efficiency, product reliability and industrial scalability.
The initiative also aims to bridge the gap between technological development and commercial production by supporting pilot manufacturing lines and industrial demonstration activities.
The funding comes as Europe’s solar manufacturing sector continues to face significant challenges. A
report by the EU’s Clean Energy Technology Observatory
found that the bloc’s manufacturing capacity for solar ingots, wafers, cells and modules remains well below the targets set under the Net-Zero Industry Act. The report estimated EU production capacity at 12 GW for modules and 2 GW for cells, highlighting the need for coordinated policy support and investment in large-scale, automated manufacturing facilities.
The European Commission has also been supporting solar manufacturing through other funding mechanisms. In October, French manufacturer Holosolis
secured support under the EU Innovation Fund
for its planned 5 GW solar cell and module factory in Hambach, France. The project was among 77 net-zero technology initiatives selected for a combined €3.4 billion in funding, including investments in solar, battery and other clean-energy manufacturing technologies.

title: Indonesia could reach 96.7 GW of solar by 2029 with policy reforms - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
IESR says Indonesia could achieve most of its 100 GW of solar by 2029 target through coordinated utility-scale procurement, rooftop PV deployment, diesel replacement and rural electrification, but warns regulatory and grid barriers need to be addressed.
Patrick Jowett
19 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Research & Development
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Highlights
Indonesia
Residential
Utility-scale
Indonesia’s cumulative installed solar capacity reached 1.59 GW as of the first quarter of 2026 (Q1 2026), according to the latest report from the Institute for Essential Services Reform (IESR), a Jakarta-based think tank.
Indonesia Solar Energy Outlook 2027
says the figure is equivalent to around 1.5% of Indonesia’s power generation capacity and 0.3% of electricity production.
Rooftop PV currently accounts for the largest share of installed capacity, standing at 0.9 GW as of Q1 2026. Utility-scale solar accounted for 0.33 GW, captive solar for 0.3 GW and installations in remote areas for around 0.06 GW.
With the country passing the 1 GW solar milestone
, IESR says the current growth rate is “far behind the government’s ambition to make solar power one of the backbones of the national energy system”, as set out in the country’s
100 GW solar power program
which President Prabowo Subianto has set a target of
achieving by 2029
The program officially launched in August with a first phase of 14 projects totalling around 5.2 GW, but only 526 MW of this capacity currently have targeted completion dates, IESR’s report reveals.
The think tank adds that deployments are currently held back by regulatory gaps, procurement uncertainty and limited grid access.
In a statement sent to
pv magazine
, IESR CEO Fabby Tumiwa said the 100 GW ambition needs to be reflected in updates to Indonesia’s 2025-2034 electricity supply business plan (RUPTL), with greater emphasis on utility-scale PV and battery energy storage systems (BESS), diesel replacement with solar-plus-storage and rooftop PV deployment.
IESR’s modelling suggests Indonesia could reach 96.7 GW of solar capacity by 2029 if development proceeds through multiple channels simultaneously.
The report says around 8 GW is already planned through RUPTL and
Mentari GigaOne
procurements, while a further 56 GW could come through procurements by Indonesia’s state-owned electric utility PLN. It suggests the remaining 33 GW could be developed through rooftop PV, diesel replacement, rural electrification, captive solar and other distributed applications.
IESR says five enablers that must move together – demand, rooftop access, procurement, grid and supply chain – will determine whether the 100 GW scales.
Under a high-electrification scenario, Indonesia’s electricity demand could be around 160 TWh higher in 2035 than under a business-as-usual scenario, according to figures from the report. Electrification of transport, industry, cooling, cooking and data centers, alongside potential electricity exports, could help create additional demand for solar generation.
IESR also suggests rooftop solar quotas be determined according to grid hosting capacity at the substation level, rather than through the current quota system, which it said limits deployment.
For utility-scale projects, the report recommends more transparent procurement schedules and reverse auctions. Projects are frequently tendered individually without a clear timetable, making it harder for developers, lenders and suppliers to prepare, IESR said.
Grid and storage investment will also need to keep pace. Indonesia’s 2025-2034 RUPTL includes 42.6 GW of renewable energy and 10.3 GW of energy storage, but some transmission infrastructure needed to integrate solar is not scheduled until 2030-2034. IESR’s report recommends regulatory changes and incentives to encourage investment in storage.
In the report, Tumiwa notes that Indonesia’s domestic solar supply chain is rising faster than demand. Solar module production capacity reached 27 GW per year in 2026, although the report notes more than half of it needs further verification due to relabelling allegations, while cell capacity now stands at 14.3 GW.
It says that after 98.2% of Indonesia’s solar module exports went to the United States in 2025, US preliminary duties of about 104% in February 2026 cut Indonesian exports to the US by about 98%, from a peak of 2.2 GW in November 2025 to 34 MW in April 2026. Final duties of up to 268% followed in September 2026
IESR says the 100 GW programme “could provide a market anchor [for the solar supply chain] if accompanied by consistent policy and project certainty”.
The 100 GW target must also be explicitly incorporated into revisions of the National Electricity General Plan (RUKN) and RUPTL, IESR added, with defined procurement channels, grid requirements, distributed solar roles and legal frameworks for project ownership and financing.

title: 10,000-hour test at 300–470°F reveals aging in nuclear fuel storage alloy
content: Researchers from the Korea Institute of Materials Science (KIMS) have discovered that aluminum alloy used to store spent nuclear fuel loses strength and is prone to degradation when exposed to temperatures exceeding 300 degrees Fahrenheit (°F) for a prolonged period.​During the experiments, the team noted that after about 10,000 hours of exposure to temperatures between 300-470°F (150-240°C), nanoscale changes occurred in the storage material. These microstructural transformations lowered the strength and hardness of the alloy, making them unsuitable for long-term storage of the nuclear fuel waste.Challenges of long-term storageExisting methods for storing spent (used) nuclear fuel after it has been removed from a reactor include interim dry storage. Instead of keeping the fuel in water-filled cooling pools, it is placed inside large, sealed metal-and-concrete containers called dry casks.​The fuel is still hot because it continues to produce decay heat (heat from the radioactive decay of leftover radioactive materials). The casks are designed to release this heat naturally through air circulation, so they don’t need water for cooling.​Moreover, inside each cask are metal support structures, such as basket rails and shims, which hold the fuel assemblies securely, keep them properly spaced for safety, and remain inside the cask for decades. Because these parts are continuously exposed to heat and cannot be easily inspected or replaced after the cask is sealed, researchers need to know how their strength and other material properties will change over many years.​This is where the latest research, led by Senior Researcher Junho Lee of the Department of Nuclear Safety Research at KIMS, comes in.​”To safely store spent nuclear fuel over long periods, it is important to understand not only the initial performance of internal components but also exactly how the materials change over time,” said Lee.Predicting decades of aging​Our study reveals how nanoscale changes within the material lead to actual strength degradation and provides a basis for predicting material performance decades into the future, he added.​In addition to providing experimental data on how the material’s properties change after more than a year (417 days, equivalent to 10,000 hours) of exposure to higher temperatures, the researchers also proposed a new accelerated aging method to evaluate its behavior over a decade.​They developed a model that uses high-temperature tests to predict how the alloy will age over decades under normal storage conditions. The team exposed the aluminum material to much higher temperatures for shorter durations. These experiments accelerated the aging process while establishing a time–temperature equivalence relationship in which similar degradation states occur under different combinations of temperature and exposure time.​The new approach, according to the researchers, would help them predict any internal changes in the material’s properties without actually performing decade-long storage tests. These results are expected to offer valuable insights for the safe long-term storage of spent nuclear fuel without actual testing.​The study provides a way to predict how materials inside spent nuclear fuel storage casks will age over decades, helping ensure long-term safety and supporting the inspections, safety assessments, and regulatory approvals needed for future dry storage systems.The findings were published in the International Journal of Energy Research.
