title: Muir Mhòr floating wind farm secures Scottish Government consent
content:
The Scottish Government has announced that the 1 GW Muir
Mhòr floating offshore wind farm
has been granted consent, allowing the project to progress to its next
The decision marks a significant milestone, as Muir Mhòr is one of the
first commercial-scale floating wind farms planned for Scottish waters.
The project is being developed by Fred. Olsen Seawind, which has nearly
three decades of experience in Scotland's renewable energy sector. Once
completed, the wind farm will consist of up to 67 offshore wind turbines
located 63 km off the coast of Aberdeenshire.
According to the announcement, consent was granted subject to several conditions,
including measures to mitigate impacts on commercial fisheries and environmental
compensation to address potential effects on seabird populations.
The company said the project will support local supply chains and contribute
millions of pounds to the regional economy. To date, £18.4 million has
been awarded through development contracts.
Public Service Reform Secretary Ivan McKee said: "This is an important
milestone for Scotland's offshore wind ambitions, with Muir Mhòr offering
significant potential to strengthen energy security, drive down floating
offshore wind costs and unlock investment and jobs."
Martha Lovatt, deputy project director for Muir Mhòr Offshore Wind Farm,
said: "Today's decision is the culmination of years of intensive environmental
assessments, technical work and constructive engagement with local communities,
marine stakeholders and industry partners.”
TGS | 4C Floating offshore Analyst Aruneesh Lakshmanavelu said: “With
the project now having both onshore and offshore consent, this good news
for Scottish renewable energy security, and good news for commercial scale
floating offshore wind development. However, Scottish consenting timelines
for offshore wind have been severely delayed, with this project taking
23 months to gain offshore consent."

content:
The UK Government has launched Allocation Round 8 (AR8) of its Contracts
for Difference (CfD) scheme with a placeholder budget of £1 for Offshore
Wind, alongside equivalent budgets for Solar PV, Onshore Wind and Floating
Offshore Wind technologies.
Rather than setting a material budget in advance, the Government said it
will review bids submitted into the auction before deciding how much funding
to allocate. Any final budget decisions will be taken with HM Treasury
and will be based on affordability and value for consumers.
AR8 is the first CfD auction in which bid stack visibility will apply across
both wind and solar technology pots. According to the announcement the
Government will assess anonymous bids submitted to Pots 1-4 before confirming
final budget levels.
The Government has also confirmed that Administrative Strike Prices will
remain unchanged from Allocation Round 7. Capacity caps will not apply
to any technology pot in AR8.
Separate clearing prices will continue to apply to offshore wind projects
in Scotland and those in England and Wales. The measure is intended to
reduce the risk of overcompensation caused by fluctuations in transmission
and distribution network charges.
TGS | 4C Senior Analyst Jordan May commented: “The government's aim in
this Allocation Round is to ensure that the clearing price is one that
consumers and industry benefit from, i.e. one that lowers their bills,
instead of adding on policy costs.”
“Historically, the goal has been to rapidly expand the fleet of renewables
to replace aging fossil generators, which requires a different strategy.
When the final price is the goal, not high volumes at the lowest price,
then a budget is somewhat meaningless, especially when costs are on the
“I am still confident that we will see a meaningful Allocation Round 8
clearing around 4-6 GW of offshore wind, likely on the lower end of the
estimate.”

title: NKT expands Isabella installation barge for ultra-shallow water operations
content:
NKT has announced that its nearshore installation barge, NKT Isabella,
has been expanded to enhance its capabilities and efficiency in nearshore
operations.
The vessel's width has been increased from 32 metres to 40 metres, allowing
space for the installation of cable-handling equipment. According to NKT,
the upgrade will support operations by helping the barge maintain a low
draft when working in ultra-shallow waters.
NKT Isabella will also be equipped with three cable turntables with a combined
capacity of 6,000 tonnes and accommodation for up to 73 offshore wind specialists.
The barge will continue to undergo further modifications as it moves closer
to joining NKT's marine installation fleet.

wind sector.

title: Will Anthropic’s IPO Lead To An Exodus of Anthropic Employees?
content: Today is a major milestone for Anthropic . The five-year-old maker of Claude beat its archrival OpenAI to the public markets, and many of its employees are going to become millionaires, if not billionaires, when the company starts to trade later today. The big question is what today means for Anthropic’s future. Before we get to that, let’s set the scene. Anthropic priced the offering at $83 a share , well  above its preliminary pricing range, valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion. Chances are the stock will trade significantly higher when it opens later Thursday. For employees looking to cash in, they’ll need the stock to stay higher for a while. While they can sell up to 10% of their shares on the first day of trading, they can’t sell more until the company reports its full-year 2026 earnings early next year. Assuming the stock doesn’t tank, the sudden influx of money will help Anthropic employees buy houses and donate a big chunk of their newfound wealth to causes like shrimp welfare . Counterintuitively, though, it may also lead them to leave the very company that brought them the wealth in the first place. You may think that employees at a company as philosophically driven as Anthropic are as bought in as the cofounders and in it for the long haul. That’s not necessarily true. At the end of the day, many of the employees, especially those who have joined more recently from big tech companies, might not be drinking the Kool-Aid as much as just trying to make a quick buck. Take Jacob Coxon , a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher who made headlines in September when he quit his job over concerns that AI “could kill us all.” When asked by Stanford political science professor Robert Reich earlier this month why he wouldn’t give up his OpenAI equity if he was so concerned about the potentially dangerous actions of AI labs, he responded, “I like money, bro. I agree it's blood money.” (After the interview, Coxon seemed to walk back his statements and pledged in a post on X to give away his OpenAI equity to charity when it goes public.) That’s an extreme example, but I’m sure a not-insignificant number of Anthropic employees wouldn’t mind taking their newfound wealth and taking a nice, long vacation on a beach somewhere! Another option for these staffers is joining another AI lab. I’ve heard of multiple instances of employees leaving one AI developer for another so they can diversify their own personal holding of equity in these companies. That way, if it’s not Anthropic that wins the AI race, but OpenAI, they’ll still be fine. Losing a significant number of researchers would not bode well for Anthropic. One of the reasons why the company has been so successful thus far is because of its low turnover. (The company said in its S-1 that it had experienced only 1% “regrettable attrition” of its employees in the last 12 months—an impressive figure!) And, if these researchers were to go to rival labs, they could bring their proprietary knowledge with them. Anthropic’s ability to retain staff is one of the many issues that investors will be watching once Anthropic is public. Even assuming Anthropic easily replaces anyone who leaves, by hiring (as it has already done) from other tech firms, there will be an impact. Outsiders will likely bring new perspectives and cultures that could clash against Anthropic’s existing culture. Today is the first day of Anthropic’s new life: let’s see how it goes. Here’s what else is going on… Overheard In Nvidia’s all-hands meeting Wednesday, interim CEO Colette Kress tried to soothe employees and prevent a potential talent exodus, The Information reported. She told employees that they can expect pay raises and more equity at the end of this year. Kress’ remarks come after more than 10,000 people who said they were Nvidia employees signed an unofficial petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. Tencent President Martin Lau said Wednesday that Washington’s new rule barring Chinese companies from accessing Nvidia ’s advanced AI chips through overseas data centers “sets everyone back in China”. The new rule, Lau said, could slow the development of new models. Wall Street executives and the National Security Agency told Congress that tech outages this week stemmed from attempts to patch security vulnerabilities identified with AI, not from cyberattacks, according to the Washington Sun. Meta Platforms has paused plans to issue a new class of shares that could help it raise more capital for AI spending as it contends with pending shareholder lawsuits. The company will not issue the new Class C shares while the legal battle plays out, it said in a court filing on Wednesday. Policy Watch The Trump administration is weighing requiring U.S. companies to disclose their use of Chinese AI models, possibly as a way to discourage the increasing use of open-weight Chinese models which can be cheaper than their closed U.S. counterparts, Reuters reported. California Governor Gavin Newsom released a proposal that would give California broad powers to impose safety measures on an AI company, Politico reported. The measure would allow state officials to intervene if they judge AI models at risk of escaping human control, require independent evaluators inside labs, and shut down AI models in emergencies. Deals and Debuts See The Information’s Generative AI Database for an exclusive list of private companies and their investors. Anthropic on Wednesday said it raised $81 billion in its initial public offering after pricing the IPO at $83 a share, above its marketed range of $70 to $78 a share, the largest in history. Anthropic sold 956.4 million shares and the seven co-founders sold 23.6 million shares for $83 each. This gives the company a fully diluted valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion. Palo Alto Networks plans to acquire Applied Compute , an AI startup founded by three former OpenAI researchers, for $4.5 billion in stock, the companies announced Wednesday. It's the latest in a string of deals by the cybersecurity giant as it aims to serve as an all-in-one provider for companies seeking to use AI safely. Sierra , which makes AI customer service agents, is in talks to raise about $1.5 billion at a valuation of about $30 billion, The Information reported. Lightspeed Venture Partners , Greenoaks and Benchmark are in talks to invest. MegaRobo , which automates science labs with robots and AI, raised nearly $200 million in a funding round joined by the Oman Investment Authority. Moonshot AI , the Beijing-based developer of the Kimi models, has scrapped a $150 million deal to access Nvidia Blackwell chips through a data center in Indonesia, after the U.S. this week announced a rule to restrict Chinese companies from accessing advanced chips remotely, The Information reported on Wednesday. BrightAI , which uses AI to monitor utility and industrial equipment, raised $97 million in a funding round led by Smith Point Capital. Linq , which builds messaging tools for AI agents, raised $90 million in a funding round led by Andreessen Horowitz. Pulley , a San Francisco-based AI construction startup, announced $64 million in new funding, including a $41 million Series B round and a $23 million Series A round from investors like Jump Capital , Catalyst Investors , CRV and Susa Ventures . Arva AI , a New York City- and London-based startup that develops agents for banking operations, raised $20 million in Series A funding led by Arthur Ventures Vero Security , which secures companies’ A.I tools and agents, raised $11 million in a seed funding round led by TLV Partners. Voyage Labs , a Menlo Park, Calif.-based startup building a personal AI agent that plans and books trips and local outings, raised $12 million in seed funding led by Kleiner Perkins . Botsync , which makes robots for factories and warehouses, raised $11 million in a funding round led by IvyCap Ventures. Google released Gemini 4 Neon , a model designed to be faster than its most powerful public model Gemini 4 Carbon and with deeper reasoning than Gemini 4 Hydrogen . The model is built for efficient cyber defense, Google said, with improved safety guardrails and behavior from Carbon. OpenAI on Wednesday published new results highlighting the growing capabilities of its AI models in chip design , reporting significant improvements to both its in-house Jalapeño chip and Advanced Micro Devices ’ flagship graphics processing unit designs. U.S. banks including JPMorgan and Citigroup have sought protection against violations of semiconductor export bans in a loan they are considering for Bridge Data Centres , a Singapore-based data center operator that once hosted Megaspeed , the firm at the center of the widening Jensen Huang scandal, according to Bloomberg. The AI Futures Project , a nonprofit that forecasts how AI may impact the future, released a proposal for how AI companies could limit and disclose how much computing power they allocate to research, slowing the pace of AI development to prioritize safety. title: Anthropic Is Pushing New Products, and Big Discounts, to Justify Its Huge Valuation
content: To justify its enormous new valuation as a public company, Anthropic needs to show that it can expand quickly in other areas of business the way it did with coding. Its early efforts are showing signs of promise—and highlighting the steep challenges it faces. Anthropic is gaining traction with Claude Cowork, an AI tool for nontechnical business users, and persuading some customers to spend in new areas such as cybersecurity. The company is also hoping to embed itself deeper in companies’ core operations with Claude Managed Agents, a set of tools that developers can use to build and run agents without having to manage the underlying servers and other infrastructure. At the same time, intensifying competition has prompted Anthropic to offer deep discounts to customers willing to devote a certain percentage of their AI budgets to the startup—and show documents to prove it, according to managers at the customers and software licensing experts. And in many new product areas, Anthropic faces more entrenched competition than it did when its Claude Code product took the business world by storm starting late last year. OpenAI is also targeting cybersecurity as a major growth area, for example, and Anthropic’s push this month into office productivity apps such as spreadsheets and brainstorming tools puts it in direct competition with Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace, products from two tech giants that are also major financial backers of Anthropic. Vertice, a software procurement firm, said that Anthropic has begun offering some credits worth up to $100,000 for its products as companies in recent months have started expanding their usage beyond engineering teams running Claude Code to Claude Cowork for sales, finance, human resources and marketing teams. The credits are offered in exchange for customers signing higher yearlong spending commitments or agreeing to sign those contracts by a certain date, said Vertice CEO Eldar Tuvey. But customers are also wary about the prospect of a surge in spending on Anthropic’s products and are looking for ways to monitor and in some cases pare back high spending as they adopt Claude Cowork, Tuvey said. Investors appear optimistic. Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 a share late Wednesday, well above its marketed range of $70 to $78 last week. That makes it the biggest IPO ever , gives Anthropic a fully diluted valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion, and will rank the five-year-old AI developer among the biggest publicly traded U.S. companies. Many analysts and investors ahead of Anthropic’s first day of trading Thursday were expecting the share price to jump further. Beyond Claude Code Anthropic was well behind OpenAI in revenue before Claude Code caught fire. Anthropic’s revenue surged to $4.7 billion in the first quarter of this year—more than all of last year—then grew 144% from that level in the second quarter. That pace has slowed, with third-quarter revenue rising 47% from the second quarter to $17 billion. Anthropic doesn’t break out sales by products or industries, but most customer spending is still geared toward Claude Code, according to customers and consultants. Anthropic’s IPO prospectus says that the top 5% of enterprise customers that use Claude Code spend about 20 times as much per month as those that don’t use the coding tool. The company has told investors that its efforts to diversify revenue are going well. Adoption of Claude Cowork—which debuted in preview in January and launched widely in April—has outpaced that of Claude Code in the nine months after the coding tool debuted in February 2025, it said, without providing figures. Anthropic has launched tailored Claude-powered tools and features for seven sectors—financial services, financial advisers, healthcare, life sciences, legal, education and government—and for broader business functions: Claude Security, Claude Design and Claude Science. Its next big use case is arguably cybersecurity. Eric Foster, CEO of TENEX.AI, an Anthropic consulting partner, said his large enterprise clients in recent months have shifted 10% to 20% of their Anthropic spending toward scanning and patching vulnerabilities in their code repositories to defend against potential hacks. They previously spent their Anthropic budget entirely on coding. Still, those customers are generally using the models with their own harnesses—software tools to manage the underlying model—rather than using Claude Security directly, indicating Anthropic may have to fight for customers to use its applications. Claude Managed Agents, another major new product, is still in public beta, but some Anthropic partners have already set it up for customers. Jamie Shepard, president of Enabuild, a consultancy that works with Anthropic customers in regulated industries like healthcare, said Claude Managed Agents has been a primary driver of a roughly 65% increase in sales prospects his firm has seen over the past few months. This adoption could benefit Anthropic. Claude Managed Agents comes with its own harness that controls how Claude agents access external data, remember previous conversations and navigate the series of steps involved in completing tasks. Agents require a high degree of customization, and once customers adopt Anthropic’s harness, it becomes more difficult for them to switch to a different provider, Shepard said. Discounts With Strings Attached While Claude Code’s runaway success largely caught rivals off guard, big competitors are already vying for many of the same new opportunities that Anthropic is pursuing. OpenAI President Greg Brockman, for example, told The Information this month that there is “no question” that cybersecurity will become a bigger business for OpenAI than coding. And the leap in spending on Anthropic and other pricey AI products this year has prompted many companies to look to lower-cost alternatives. Customers including FedEx, Robinhood, Coinbase and Shopify have developed their own software for coding that allows them to easily switch between Anthropic, OpenAI and open-source models. And OpenAI’s efforts to undercut Anthropic’s prices have swayed some firms to use OpenAI’s coding tool, Codex. Robust competition, customer cost concerns and the relative ease of switching AI models have prompted Anthropic to employ various tactics to woo new customers and keep others in the fold. Anthropic gave clients credits of up to $2,000 per user to test Claude Cowork, Claude Design and Claude Security when they were introduced, according to a partner of the AI firm that works with about 1,000 of its large enterprise customers. Anthropic also appears more open about giving large customers bigger discounts than it has in the past, according to managers from two customers. In at least two instances, the discounts it offered were larger than 30%, said the managers. One said that level of discount was more than double what Anthropic had given his firm in its prior agreement. OpenAI, meanwhile, has offered discounts higher than the 20% to 30% that some founders said they received on listed prices for its models—in at least one case, 40% to get a company to switch from competing AI coding tools to Codex. Anthropic is trying to ensure that its discounts lead to lasting business. To get them, some customers have to agree to earmark a certain percentage of overall AI spending for Anthropic, under what is known as a “share-of-wallet” clause, said the managers from the two customers. More recently, Anthropic has started asking some customers to show their invoices and other documents to prove they are meeting these terms, said Madisyn Ellsworth, an analyst at NPI Financial, a firm that helps companies negotiate contracts with Anthropic and other software providers. NPI first noticed this language in Anthropic’s agreements in early November, said Ellsworth. While OpenAI also includes share-of-wallet clauses in some of its contracts, NPI hasn’t seen any instances where the ChatGPT maker is asking customers to produce documentation, she added. One software firm said Anthropic has moved from a discount of around 15% on listed token prices for a $1 million spending commitment in the first quarter to nearly 30% after the firm agreed to spend $3 million over the summer. Most of the increased spending came from human resources, finance and sales teams using Claude Cowork to perform tasks such as generating financial forecasts and preparing market research reports. While the company spent more than 90% of its Anthropic budget on engineering tasks earlier this year, 60% now goes to coding and around 40% to Claude Cowork as well as tools like Claude Design and Claude Security for niche projects. Anthropic told the software firm it would offer a discount higher than 30% if the company committed to spending more than $5 million annually.

title: China’s Moonshot AI Scraps $150 Million Deal to Access Nvidia Chips in Indonesia
content: Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based developer of the Kimi models, has scrapped a $150 million deal to access Nvidia Blackwell chips through a data center in Indonesia, after the U.S. this week announced a rule to restrict Chinese companies from accessing advanced chips remotely, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. Moonshot signed the contract with a Southeast Asian neocloud to rent access to a sizable cluster of Blackwell Ultra B300 chips, starting from as early as next year, the people said. The B300 is one of Nvidia’s most powerful AI chips, and is barred by the U.S. government from sale to China. Chinese companies were able to access restricted Nvidia chips from data centers outside of the country, a loophole that was plugged by the rule released by the U.S. Commerce Department this week. To use the loophole, Chinese companies in the past several years signed large deals to rent data centers equipped with the state-of-the-art Nvidia chips in other countries, with Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand among the most popular locations. Under the new rule, data centers already serving Chinese customers above a certain computing threshold have 90 days to obtain a U.S. license. Moonshot’s scrapped deal in Indonesia could be a harbinger of more cancellations, particularly for projects still being built. Moonshot rose to global prominence in July after its K3 model displayed capabilities rivaling U.S. frontier models. The access to Nvidia Blackwell chips from outside of China was crucial to Moonshot’s development of the model, and the startup had been seeking more Blackwell chips for its next model, Kimi K4, The Information reported in July. Shortly after K3’s release, the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, an agency under the Department of Commerce, said it was formally investigating Moonshot’s access to advanced AI chips. In a mark of its hunger for compute, Moonshot agreed to a roughly 50% upfront payment for the $150 million deal in Indonesia, one of the people with direct knowledge said. Typical contract terms require an upfront payment of around 15%. Moonshot has also paused discussions for other new deals, as it reviews the impact from the new regulations, said the other person with direct knowledge. Moonshot declined to comment. Under the new rule, data centers outside the U.S. equipped with AI chips up to certain threshold are required to perform strict checks on customers for any ownership links to China. The U.S. also requires a license for the export of advanced chips to companies headquartered in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, countries with a high risk of diversion of chips. The computing threshold that triggers the  license requirement is exceedingly low: equivalent to roughly 300 of the most advanced AI chips on the market, according to law firm Sidley Austin . The deals that Chinese AI firms look for usually involve at least a couple thousand chips. The U.S. move formally restricts a critical compute source on which Chinese labs have long relied, throwing their AI development plans into disarray. The restriction is likely to raise the cost of training models, according to a note this week by Bernstein analysts led by Qingyuan Lin. Fears of running afoul of the new rules have also prompted bankers to reconsider lending to Chinese-linked projects. Executives at five lenders have discussed abandoning or passing on a $480 million deal for Singapore-based neocloud Aolani, meant to fund the purchase of advanced Nvidia chips for ByteDance ’s use, Bloomberg reported . The chips are slated to be housed in a data center in Malaysia.

title: U.S. Commerce Department Rushed to Clear Nvidia H200 Exports to China
content: In recent months, Jeffrey Kessler, the official overseeing the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, has pressured staff to expedite the approval of sales of Nvidia ’s H200 graphics processing units to China, according to three people with knowledge of the matter. In some cases, Kessler directed staff at BIS —an agency under the Commerce Department—to approve the exports over objections from other U.S. government departments, two of those people said. The H200, launched in 2023, is an older generation of Nvidia chips that developers can use to train and run AI models. In December 2025, President Donald Trump approved the chip, which is a generation behind Nvidia’s mainstay Blackwell product, for sale to China, after intense lobbying from former CEO Jensen Huang. As part of the approval, Nvidia agreed to give the U.S. government a 25% cut of H200 sales to China. The pressure on BIS staff to speed up the H200 approvals, which hasn’t previously been reported, could add further scrutiny to a crisis that has engulfed Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. He resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive last week after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence suspect spied for China, who also built a network of companies that move billions of dollars of restricted Nvidia chips to China. Lawmakers have since opened probes into how Commerce approved Nvidia chip sales to China, and want Huang, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and BIS chief Kessler to testify. Meanwhile, as the furor intensified, Nvidia’s current leaders this week said they pulled the plug on some chip sales to China. During the company’s Tuesday evening earnings call, interim CEO Colette Kress said the chipmaker had stopped shipping a class of export-compliant chips, which includes the H200, to China. Kress didn’t explain the reason for the decision. When it was still selling such chips in China, there was a lot of red tape Nvidia had to go through to complete such sales. Under the U.S. export rules, four departments—Commerce, State, Energy and Defense—had to rubber-stamp each export sale of H200s to Chinese buyers. Under a rule Commerce issued in January, the exporter had to certify that the chips wouldn’t go to China’s military or to blacklisted entities. Separately, U.S. export regulations required BIS to weigh the reliability of each party to a sale, such as if they can be trusted in their intended use of the chips and not passing the chips to other companies or the Chinese military. The procedure is designed to also prevent the chips from ending up in smuggling channels. Yet, Kessler, the Commerce under secretary who runs BIS, regularly pressured staff to expedite the approval without having ample opportunity to conduct due diligence on Chinese companies that submitted the export requests, the three people said. BIS issued some licenses even after reviewers’ checks turned up red flags from other departments, two of the people said. As a result, BIS granted approvals to at least two companies that have ties to the Chinese military or state-owned enterprises, or were involved in the smuggling of Nvidia Blackwell chips into China, according to people with direct knowledge and a review of these companies’ registration records. The Commerce Department expedited H200 licensing because processing the licenses was a priority for the Trump administration, said a separate person familiar with the matter, who added that the recipients of the licenses were still subject to the same national security conditions and due diligence process. Nvidia, for its part, said its H200 sales to customers in China went through the appropriate government approval process. “The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China,” said an Nvidia spokesperson. For at least some H200 licenses, Kessler took the position that the usual interagency review wasn’t needed, according to the two people with knowledge of the matter. That review dates to an executive order signed by President Bill Clinton in 1995. It lets the State, Defense and Energy departments weigh in on export license applications alongside Commerce, and sets up a formal appeals process for when they disagree. In some cases, BIS stepped in to approve export licenses for customers seeking Nvidia H200s even when other agencies refused to sign off on those applications, one of the two people said. Questionable Approvals One of the companies that received an H200 license is Zhejiang Yindun Cloud Technology, which is tied to Range Intelligent Computing Technology Group, a Shenzhen-listed data center operator, according to one of the two people and two separate people familiar with the matter. Range buys powerful Nvidia chips from companies involved in the smuggling network and rents them to local tech firms, two of the three people said. Yindun was controlled by the family members of an executive at Range until June 2026, when the ownership was transferred to companies controlled by the Tibetan government, according to corporate registration records and two people close to the company. Another licensee, Shanghai LinkWise, operates in a data center built by a company tied to the Chinese navy. LinkWise became a partner in an undersea data center in Shanghai in 2025, according to a Shanghai government announcement , and has since moved in. The data center developer’s largest shareholder is Beijing Highlander Digital Technology, which has been a supplier to China’s navy since 2004— according to the company’s website —and which was put on a U.S. trade blacklist in 2022. LinkWise’s website says it has developed specialized shipping containers that each can host 16 Nvidia Blackwell servers, though it is unclear whether the company has any of the servers. The push to approve chip sales to China didn’t extend to Nvidia’s main rival. Leaders at BIS didn’t rush staffers to approve sales of Advanced Micro Devices’ MI325X, which has performance comparable to the H200’s and which was also cleared by Trump for exports to China, according to one person with knowledge of the situation. “Export controls should evolve with changes in technology, while protecting national security,” Kessler said in a statement when the rule was issued in January. “Permitting the sale of the H200 to China under controlled conditions will strengthen the American technology ecosystem.” A U.S. export license only clears part of the hurdle for Chinese companies to access the H200. Beijing has been resisting the H200 flooding into China to wean the country off American technology. The Chinese government in January told some tech companies it would approve H200 purchases only in special circumstances, such as for university research labs, The Information reported. Beijing later cracked the door open, approving a small batch of H200s to companies including ByteDance and Alibaba. In the meantime, Kress, Nvidia’s interim CEO, sought to downplay the financial impact that discontinuing sales of H200 and other chips to China would have on the company. On Tuesday, she told analysts that Nvidia sold $2.4 billion of licensed data center products to China from its Hopper family of chips—which includes the H200—during the fiscal third quarter. That represented only 2% of the company’s $115.8 billion in revenue during that period.

title: Anthropic’s Public Debut Looms
content: We all need a break from the Nvidia soap opera, so we’re switching things up today and talking about that other drama percolating in the background—Anthropic’s public debut. The company behind Claude priced its initial public offering on Wednesday night at $83 a share, several dollars above its preliminary pricing range, and at a level that values the whole company at around $1.5 trillion. Seeing as this is the first top AI model developer to go public, not to mention the biggest, we’d bet the stock reaches $150 when it opens on Thursday, as everyone and their dog vies for a piece of the action. Of course, if they were smart, they’d hold back. The stock is more than likely to settle lower in the next few days, as the initial burst of exuberance dissipates. As for where the stock will trade in six months, I can’t guess. The crystal ball I ordered online got stolen en route to my apartment— thanks for nothing, FedEx. (The Information on Thursday will livestream a two-hour video discussion on Anthropic’s valuation, tech, cybersecurity strategy, drug discovery ambitions, as well as market movements: Check it out , starting at 11:30 a.m. PT / 2:30 p.m. ET.) We shouldn’t assume Anthropic’s first year as a public company will be like that of another groundbreaking tech firm, Google, whose shares steadily rallied in the months after its 2004 IPO and a year later were trading more than 200% higher than its IPO price. For one thing, Google was a cash machine from its early days. In 2004, the year it went public, its free cash flow rocketed 200% from 2003 and just grew from there. Anthropic could be the opposite. It generated $5.6 billion in free cash flow in the first nine months of this year, but its business model is about to shift to one where it will generate minimal, if any, cash. That’s because Anthropic is investing in leasing chips and running them itself in its own data centers, rather than relying entirely on outside cloud firms to run its AI. That move will change “the cash flow profile of our business,” it coyly says in its IPO prospectus. It’s a smart move in the long run, giving Anthropic more control over the infrastructure that its services run on, which should help it keep costs under control. “Investors generally agree with the logic that a company this dependent on compute should be more vertically integrated,” according to research firm William Blair in a note Wednesday. But in the medium term, Anthropic has to make sure it can pay the bills. The company is also spending a fortune paying other cloud firms for computing capacity. All up, including money being spent on leasing its own chips, the company has $452 billion in purchase commitments and lease agreements due before the end of 2030. That translates to a significant annual nut for Anthropic to cover. Remember, its revenue in the first nine months of this year was $33 billion, although its annualized run rate reached $81 billion at the end of October, the company said in its IPO filings. Still, given Anthropic’s hefty commitments, it can’t afford any kind of slowdown. And yet, given the intensifying competition from other AI models—including open-source models that businesses are trying more and more as a way of improving the bang for the buck they get on AI spending—its future growth rate is anything but assured. Anthropic is truly the first of its kind—but whether it will prove a profitable business in the long run is still up in the air. For that reason, investors may do well to be careful at what price they buy the stock. Palo Alto Networks’ Latest Purchase Cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks has been on a shopping spree lately , snapping up Datadog rival Chronosphere for $3.35 billion at the start of the year and Israeli login-software firm CyberArk for $25 billion a short time later, not to mention the smaller purchases of Koi Security, Portkey and Embrace since then. But on Wednesday Palo Alto struck a different kind of deal—the purchase of Applied Compute for $4.5 billion in stock. Applied Compute isn’t a cybersecurity firm but a young startup that helps companies customize AI models with their own data. That’s a hot field, as more businesses decide they don’t want to use the leading AI models from companies like Anthropic for anything that deals with sensitive internal data, given questions about the security of that data. Meanwhile, cybersecurity is becoming a massive issue for businesses, given AI’s ability to spot holes in software. Palo Alto presumably sees Applied Compute as a way to pitch businesses on combining its skills in cybersecurity with Applied’s more secure customized models. As my colleague Aaron Holmes puts it, AI security will be increasingly handled by customized small models—which is a future that Palo Alto is now well positioned for. No wonder Palo Alto stock jumped 9% in after-hours trading on Wednesday. In Other News • Nvidia held its first employee all-hands meeting without CEO Jensen Huang on Wednesday morning, with one notable executive on stage: former sales chief Jay Puri .  More on the meeting here. • U.S. banks including JPMorgan and Citigroup have sought protection against violations of semiconductor export bans in a loan they are considering for Bridge Data Centres, a Singapore-based data center operator that once hosted Megaspeed, the firm at the center of the widening Jensen Huang scandal, according to Bloomberg. • Tencent President Martin Lau said Wednesday that Washington’s new rule barring Chinese companies from accessing Nvidia’s advanced AI chips through overseas data centers “sets everyone back in China.” • Meta Platforms is delaying distributing a new class of shares while a lawsuit filed by investors opposed to the plan plays out, Bloomberg reported. title: Bret Taylor’s Sierra in Talks to Raise at $30 Billion Valuation
content: Sierra, the AI customer support startup founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, has been in talks to raise new funding at around a $30 billion valuation, according to two people with knowledge of the fundraise. That price would nearly double the $15 billion-plus valuation it received in its last round announced in May. The three-year old startup is discussing raising around $1.5 billion in new funding, one of the people said.  Lightspeed Venture Partners, Greenoaks and Benchmark are in talks to invest, the person said. The talks are still early and terms could change. The potential fundraising highlights continued investor interest in startups that are building AI applications and that are seeing rapid revenue growth and pulling ahead of competitors. San Francisco-based Sierra said last month that it had surpassed $400 million in annualized revenue, doubling its revenue pace from just five months prior. A spokesperson didn’t respond to requests for comment. Meanwhile, Decagon, a top rival to Sierra, was generating around $100 million in annualized revenue at the end of the second quarter and projecting between $175 million and $200 million in annualized revenue by year’s end, said a separate person who has spoken with Decagon executives. Decagon has recently been speaking with investors about raising hundreds of millions in new funding, the person said, though its valuation target couldn’t be learned. Sierra and Decagon have historically differentiated from each other by going after different types of customers. While Sierra serves larger companies such as JP Morgan Chase, Cigna and Liberty Global, Decagon has targeted startups and smaller businesses like Perplexity, Notion and Duolingo. More recently, Decagon has added larger customers like Delta, American Airlines, Hertz, Avis and Deutsche Telekom, according to a person with knowledge of the business. AI applications like Sierra and Decagon have seen rapid revenue growth during the AI boom, as businesses rush to try new tools. However, many of these startups have not seen the 70%-plus gross margins that traditional software businesses have enjoyed. Their margins are hit by the high costs of frontier models, though AI model developers such as OpenAI have been aggressively slashing prices in recent months. Additionally, many AI app startups like Sierra also hire technical consultants, sometimes called forward deployed engineers, that work closely with businesses  to help them customize Sierra’s tech for their specific applications. Such employees can also be costly and negatively affect gross margins depending on how a startup categorizes such costs. (Sierra’s gross margins couldn’t be learned.) Sierra has previously raised more than $1.5 billion in funding from investors including Tiger Global Management, GV, Greenoaks, Sequoia Capital and Benchmark.

title: How to Diagnose a Recurring Technical Problem with Google Gemini
content: Persistent IT problems can drain employee productivity and strain help desk teams. And while a  one-off technology problem often amounts to little more than a nuisance, recurring problems often have a real impact on the business. Imagine, for instance, that you run IT support for your company, and employees keep reporting that their VPN connections are dropping, locking remote workers out of company systems. Even with your IT team helping one user after another, the tickets keep piling up, and the underlying issue remains unaddressed. Google Gemini can help IT teams sort through this information, spot patterns, and identify the root of the problem to help the organization get back to business. Step 1: Define the Problem First, you’ll want to use Gemini to cut through the chaos of helpdesk logs to better understand the frequency of the issue and create a consolidated dataset for further analysis. Take a screenshot of the error message that your users are getting, and export data from recent support tickets into a Google Sheet. Then, ask Gemini to compare the ticket data against the error message. Try this prompt: You are a Level 2 debugging specialist. Analyze the attached error screenshot to identify the exact error code or message. Using this key, review the attached support tickets from the last 60 days and find all tickets that contain the identical error message. Output the results as a table. Step 2: Hunt for Root Cause From a dataset of 500 help tickets, Gemini might identify two dozen or so dropped VPN connections, providing a table that identifies the ticket number, date, and location of each. This narrower dataset will make it easier to find out what the tickets have in common (and, therefore, what might be causing the problem). Your ticket export should already include each employee’s operating system, VPN client version, and location. To see what the affected employees have in common, prompt Gemini again: You are a technical data analyst. Analyze the consolidated ticket data to identify statistically significant correlations between the ‘VPN connection dropping’ issue and the following attributes: operating system, VPN client version, and user geolocation. Format the findings as a ranked list, stating the calculated confidence level for each correlation. The results of this step can be extremely revealing. For example, Gemini might note that only macOS users running a particular client version are experiencing the problem. Step 3: Identify the Solution The good news is that your helpdesk team has already solved users’ VPN problem multiple times. However, it’s likely this is the first time anyone has looked at all of these tickets together, since they were previously scattered among tickets for various one-off problems. Therefore, it’s highly possible no one in the organization knows the most common fix, even if your helpdesk has already applied that solution over and over again. In your Gemini chat, type: From the ‘Resolution Notes’ field of all closed tickets in the consolidated data, extract and rank the top 5 most successful, non-escalated troubleshooting actions that resolved the ‘VPN connection dropping’ issue. Output the steps as a numbered list, including the calculated frequency/success rate for each step. Gemini will identify which fixes have been tried and list their success rates. For example, Gemini might note that every resolved ticket required the user to install a new client version and clear the macOS DNS cache. Step 4: Create a Playbook Now that you know how often VPN connections are dropping, what is causing the problem, and how it has been fixed in the past, you can give your frontline technicians a clear, repeatable playbook for handling the issue. This will ensure that the problem gets fixed quickly, without unnecessary escalation to senior engineers. Gemini can quickly draft a playbook with desired content, length, and tone. Try this prompt: You are a Level 2 technical writer. Draft an updated, internal-facing knowledge base article titled ‘Resolving recurring VPN drops: root cause analysis and Tier 1 triage.’ Structure the article with two main sections: ‘Summary of root cause’ and ‘Tier 1 troubleshooting steps.’ The tone must be concise and instructional, explicitly targeting Level 1 helpdesk technicians. The playbook will give your technicians exactly the information they’ll need when the issue pops up again in the future. And a problem that previously robbed teams of hours of productive time each month will instead be resolved in minutes.

title: ‘Theranos But Real’: New Blood-Testing Startup Says It Can Predict Health Risks
content: With all the renewed interest around the saga of Theranos, two startup founders, Omar Abudayyeh and Jonathan Gootenberg, made the tongue-in-cheek decision to plunk down about $12 for the rights to the URL: theranosbutworks.com . That URL redirects to the main website for their 16-month-old health- and blood-testing company, Helios, which is coming out of stealth on Wednesday. With just a drop of blood drawn from a small, needle-free device, Abudayyeh, 36, and Gootenberg, 35, say the company can measure over 1,000 proteins within someone’s body that provide insight into their current state of health and predictions about a person’s risk of diseases like heart failure, blood cancers and Alzheimer’s disease over the next 10 years. Abudayyeh and Gootenberg worked on Helios at Y Combinator earlier this year with a third co-founder, Yousef Badran, a scientist and doctor at Massachusetts General Hospital. When they went to raise money, several prospective investors made the same comment, Abudayyeh recalled: “This sounds like Theranos—but real. We would love to chat.” They ended up with $2.3 million in seed funding from Y Combinator, venture firm Formation and angel investors. Helios is one of several companies pursuing what’s called proteomics testing, which measures the proteins continually made by cells, tissues and organs. Illumina bought the proteomics company SomaLogic earlier this year, and Thermo Fisher Scientific acquired proteomics company Olink in 2024. Vero Bioscience, spun out of the Stanford lab of scientist Tony Wyss-Coray, is developing a blood test that measures proteins and calculates the biological age of different organs. Pharma companies utilize proteomics in drug development, and academic and medical centers use it for disease research and diagnoses. Finding ways for consumers to routinely use the information is drawing attention lately, in part because of growing interest in longevity science. The proteins can give people a real-time snapshot of their health, and a way to track if lifestyle changes or other interventions are making a difference. Proteomics can help people spot heart or other health problems that don’t show up on standard blood tests, offering a chance to intervene early. Helios’ blood test. Photo by Helios There has also been a lot of excitement about proteomics after Novo Nordisk gave a presentation in October at the Aging Research & Drug Discovery conference. The company said it drew blood samples from people when they enrolled in clinical trials of its weight-loss drugs Ozempic and Wegovy and then again months later. The company used proteomics analyses to determine patients taking the drugs had slower aging in their organs compared to people who got a placebo. Proteomics involves a different technology from what Theranos employed. Theranos claimed its machine could run hundreds of standard blood tests using only a small amount of blood. In the Nathan Fielder movie about the Theranos scandal, “You Can See Everything,” Elizabeth Holmes and her romantic partner Billy Evans are depicted pitching potential investors about a “Theranos 2.0” idea. Evans is the founder of Austin, Texas-based diagnostics startup Haemanthus, which in a New York Times article is described as making a device that can test blood, urine and saliva. Helios’ device is placed on the upper arm with adhesive, and when you push a button on it, it pricks your arm to retrieve a drop of blood, which is stored on a cartridge. The device is then removed, sealed in a pouch and mailed to Helios’ lab in Boston. At the lab, the proteins are measured. Helios’ AI models then calculate how organs like the heart, liver, brain and kidneys are functioning and the risk for getting major diseases in the future. The AI agent also makes recommendations about what diet and lifestyle changes, supplements or medications can improve the scores. The algorithm makes its predictions and recommendations based on more than 80,000 scientific papers, genetic studies and clinical trial results. The test will be available at the start of 2027, initially at longevity clinics and through concierge doctors. Helios plans to charge $250 to $600 per test, depending on the volume the clinics buy. Abudayyeh and Gootenberg said they hope to sell tests directly to consumers through their website by the end of 2027. The direct-to-consumer price has not been set yet. Helios co-founders Jonathan Gootenberg (left) and Omar Abudayyeh. Photo by Helios Abudayyeh and Gootenberg met as undergraduates at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. They both ended up doing graduate studies in the lab of Feng Zhang, a pioneer of Crispr gene editing in humans. Abudayyeh and Gootenberg co-authored many papers published in prestigious academic journals related to Crispr technology and gene editing. They also co-founded five companies together prior to Helios, including Sherlock Biosciences (a Crispr diagnostics company bought in 2024 by OraSure Technologies) and Tome Biosciences (a gene-editing startup that raised over $200 million before shutting down in 2024 after running out of funds). Gootenberg, who saw “You Can See Everything” with a group that included Abudayyeh, says the incongruity of the scene where Evans and Holmes are enthusiastically describing to investors their vision for “Theranos 2.0” even as Holmes was due to soon begin serving a prison sentence stuck with him. “Even after what happened, that people would still be receptive speaks a lot to the need for these technologies, the societal need, the investor need. That was pretty striking,” Gootenberg said. “What Theranos promised and their vision is still super exciting to people and resonates,” said Abudayyeh. They made a launch video for the Helios website where Abudayyeh acknowledges, “And yes, we know technology has made big promises about a single drop of blood before,” while their scientific and academic credentials flash on the screen as a hopeful reminder that they are different. The video also points out that proteomics technology has been used and validated in labs and companies around the world. Despite the growing excitement about proteomics tests, Vero’s Wyss-Coray says he too tries to address the inevitable Theranos comparisons that come up. “When I give a talk, I say, ‘This is not Theranos,’” Wyss-Coray says. “It usually gets a laugh.”

title: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
content:
A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
Technology called “machine perfusion” is creating the chance for more transplants—and daring new science.
Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.
The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.
In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.
“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says.
Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.
Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.
Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.
Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.
While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”
Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days—the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.
Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.
What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.
Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins, the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.
For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.
“It’s important to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” says Martins. “That’s how science moves.”
He’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has said it wants to extend the time to two weeks.
Similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.
Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs, a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.
Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two new scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “organ medicine”: research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”
“What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” says Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely new.”

title: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
content:
What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
The deal between Sila and Panasonic Energy is a bright spot for the industry, and it shows how politics have shifted recently for batteries.
After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.
Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time.
This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.
Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.
We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.
Things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.
The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.
Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.
This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech, have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.
The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.
China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.
Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.)
I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority.
“I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”

IMMS und Fraunhofer IPT starten Verbundprojekt »PlanarMikroFab«: Ziel des von sieben Unternehmen der Forschungsgemeinschaft Ultrapräzisionstechnik e.V. (UPT) begleiteten und anlässlich der Herbsttagung der UPT in Aschaffenburg begonnenen Projekts ist ein leichtbauoptimierter XY-Planartisch mit integrierter Sensorik auf Basis eines planaren Direktantriebs. Das neue Antriebssystem wird sehr dynamische Bewegungen für die Herstellung äußerst komplexer Mikrostrukturen mit gleichbleibend hoher Qualität ermöglichen und diese wirtschaftlicher machen. Davon werden Anwendungen wie die Fertigung von Mikrolinsenarrays für Photonik, Medizintechnik, Halbleiter und Photovoltaik profitieren.
Das IMMS Institut für Mikroelektronik- und Mechatronik-Systeme gemeinnützige GmbH (IMMS GmbH) aus Ilmenau und das Fraunhofer-Institut für Produktionstechnologie IPT aus Aachen haben im Projektauftakttreffen am 12.11.2026 die Arbeiten zur Entwicklung einer neuartigen Positionierplattform für die Ultrapräzisionsfertigung im Verbundvorhaben »Hochdynamische Nanopositionier-Planar-Stage für Mikrofabrikations-Aufgaben« (PlanarMikroFab) aufgenommen.
Mehr Dynamik für die Mikrofertigung, höherer Druck für KMU
Moderne Optiken mit Freiformflächen und integrierten Mikrostrukturen erfordern neben exzellenter Oberflächenqualität mit Nanometergenauigkeit auch höchste Formtreue. Mit steigender Geometriekomplexität stoßen etablierte Ultrapräzisions-Werkzeugmaschinen an ihre Grenzen: Soll die Leistung von monokristallinen Diamantwerkzeugen in feinster Auflösung ausgereizt werden, braucht es Nanometer-Genauigkeit in der Bewegungsführung bei gleichzeitig höchstmöglicher Dynamik. Aktuell begrenzen die großen mitbewegten Massen, Schwingungen aus Antriebs- und Reaktionskräften und thermische Verformungen die praktisch erzielbare Vorschubdynamik erheblich, obwohl die eingesetzten Werkzeuge theoretisch deutlich mehr leisten könnten.
Die steigende Nachfrage nach individualisierten, hochpräzisen Komponenten setzt Unternehmen vermehrt unter Druck, weiterhin wirtschaftlich und qualitativ hochwertig zu produzieren. Das triff vor allem auf die wachstumsstarke Schlüsselbranche Photonik zu, die in Europa vor allem klein- und mittelständisch geprägt ist. Viele dieser KMU sind in einigen Disziplinen hochspezialisiert. Eine tiefgehende Auseinandersetzung mit den für eine neuartige Steuerungs- und Antriebstechnik notwendigen Innovationen übersteigt jedoch ihre Kapazitäten.
Das Projekt PlanarMikroFab strebt daher an, die Wettbewerbsfähigkeit von solchen KMU bezüglich Qualität, Ausbeute, Taktzeit und Serienkosten zu erhöhen sowie Spielräume zu schaffen, um komplexere Freiform-Mikrostrukturen wirtschaftlich anzubieten, die dem wachsenden Photonikmarkt entsprechen.
Planarer Direktantrieb mit Carbon-Läufer – weniger Masse, mehr Präzision
Anstatt des klassischen seriellen Achsaufbaus nutzt das Projekt einen am IMMS entwickelten planaren Direktantrieb, bei dem die Aktorkräfte parallel und direkt auf ein einziges, reibungsfrei geführtes Bauteil – den Läufer – übertragen werden. Die Aktoren fungieren somit als Antriebe und als Teil des Führungssystems. Dieses Konzept sorgt bereits für eine reduzierte mitbewegte Masse und eine verkürzte kinematische Kette und es verbessert die Regelbarkeit sowie die erzielbare Bandbreite erheblich. Zusätzlich soll der bisherige Aluminium-Läufer als Faserverbundkunststoff-Modul mit Kohlenstofffasern in einem automatisierten thermoplastischen Tape-Lege-Prozess mit In-situ-Konsolidierung in Laminatschichten gefertigt werden. Mit dem leichtbauoptimierten Läufersystem, welches das Fraunhofer IPT entwickeln wird, lässt sich nicht nur das Gewicht gegenüber einer Aluminium-Ausführung bei gleichbleibender oder gesteigerter Steifigkeit um rund 50 Prozent reduzieren. Kohlenstofffasern besitzen zudem einen negativen thermischen Ausdehnungskoeffizienten. Mit einem geeigneten Lagenaufbau lässt sich ein Ausdehnungskoeffizient nahe Null realisieren. Derart thermisch stabile Materialien sind für Ultrapräzisionsanwendungen extrem vorteilhaft.
Fasersensoren im Läufer für Echtzeitmessungen von Dehnungen
Die bei Aluminium-Läufern auf der Oberfläche platzierbaren Dehnungsmessstreifen können nur eingeschränkte Hinweise zu thermischen Verformungen des gesamten Läufers geben. Die direkt in das Carbon-Laminat des neuen Läufers integrierbaren faseroptischen Sensoren des Fraunhofer IPT werden Temperatur und Verformung unmittelbar an der bewegten Struktur hochfrequent erfassen können. Mit diesen in den Lageregelkreis einspielbaren Daten soll erstmals auch die bislang unzureichend erfasste Strecke zwischen Wegmesssystem und Werkzeugspitze regelbar werden.
Steuerung und Regelung: Vom Industriestandard zur adaptiven Störgrößenkompensation
Ein wichtiger Innovationsschritt im Projekt PlanarMikroFab liegt in der Steuerungs- und Regelungsstrategie, für die das IMMS neue Methoden entwickeln und implementieren wird. Der Industriestandard setzt bislang auf klassische Feedbackregelungen mit kaskadierten Reglern, Feedforward-Ansätze für verbesserte Bahngenauigkeit oder auch datengetriebene Tuningmethoden. Die im Projekt anvisierte robuste, nichtlineare Regelung wird eine modellbasierte Auslegung für die Streckendynamik, eine nachgeführt parametrierte Vorsteuerung für Geschwindigkeit, Beschleunigung und Kraft sowie eine adaptive Störkraftkompensation verbinden. Damit wird es möglich, werkzeuginduzierte Störungen wie Schleppfehler, Trägheitseffekte und Schwingungen sowie Unsicherheiten im Systemverhalten in Echtzeit zu minimieren. Das ist der Schlüssel, um bei hoher Bahndynamik die Formgenauigkeit und Oberflächenqualität im Nanometerbereich zu erhalten.
Transfer in die Industrie und die Photonik-Branche
Die im Verbundprojekt angestrebten Lösungen zur Fertigung qualitativ hochwertiger komplexer optischer Komponenten werden dazu beitragen, Prozesse dynamisch zu optimieren und damit im Wettbewerb mit internationalen Anbietern bestehen zu können. Mit der zu entwickelnden Methodik für eine synchronisierte Ansteuerung hochdynamischer Mehrachssysteme wird ein Modul entstehen, das in vorhandene Maschinen sowie in neue Maschinenkonzepte integriert werden und so den Innovationsvorsprung von Maschinenherstellern und produzierenden Unternehmen erhöhen kann.
Über die Photonik hinaus sollen die Ergebnisse über das Netzwerk der Forschungsgemeinschaft Ultrapräzisionstechnik und den projektbegleitenden Ausschuss aus Industrieunternehmen direkt in Maschinenbau, Steuerungs-, Antriebs- und Produktionstechnik sowie in die anwendenden Branchen übertragen werden, etwa in den Werkzeug- und Formenbau, den Maschinenbau und die Mikromontage.
Förderung
Das Verbundvorhaben »Hochdynamische Nanopositionier-Planar-Stage für Mikrofabrikations-Aufgaben« (PlanarMikroFab) wird im Rahmen der Industriellen Gemeinschaftsforschung (IGF) vom Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft und Energie unter der Nummer 01IF25605N gefördert.

Studierende aus sieben Hochschulen und ein Azubi-Team lösten beim dritten Hackathon hack4GDI_DE an der Hochschule Mainz fünf Challenges mit öffentlichen Geodaten.
Eine Augmented-Reality-App für die Bahnreise, die komfortable Planung von Radtouren, ein Bewertungssystem für Entsiegelungsflächen und eine Onlineanwendung für die Suche nach der zuständigen Behörde: Beim dritten hack4GDI_DE an der Hochschule Mainz entwickelten rund 70 Studierende am 13. und 14. November praxisnahe Lösungen auf Basis öffentlicher Geodaten. Die Teilnehmenden kamen von sieben Hochschulen, dazu trat ein Team von Auszubildenden im Bereich Geomatik an. Veranstalter waren die Koordinierungsstelle GDI-DE und die Hochschule Mainz.
Den ersten Platz sicherte sich das „Team Oldenburg“ mit seiner Bahnorama-Lösung für die Challenge „Zugbegleiter“. Die Augmented-Reality-Webapp macht aus einer passiven Bahnreise eine aktive Sightseeing-Tour mit dem eigenen Smartphone. Platz 2 ging an das Team „Pedal to the Metal“. Deren Lösung in der Challenge „Fahrradtourismus“ ermöglicht die komfortable Planung von Radreisen, inklusive Informationen zu Übernachtungsmöglichkeiten sowie zu geographischen und touristischen Routendetails. Beide Teams waren aus Oldenburg angereist.
Aufgrund der hohen Qualität der Beiträge vergab die Jury den dritten Platz gleich zweimal. Das Mainzer Team „Die 05er Entsiegler – Weck, Worscht & WMS“ zeigte in der Challenge „Flächenentsiegelung“ eine GIS-basierte Lösung, mit der sich Flächen mit Entsiegelungspotenzial in der Stadt Mainz anhand eines Bewertungssystems identifizieren lassen. Das Team „LeBeZi“ – ein gemischtes Team aus Tübinger, Augsburger und Mainzer Studierenden – kombinierte in der Challenge „Zuständigkeitsfinder“ amtliche Informationen aus unterschiedlichen Quellen und Formaten, damit Nutzende die zuständige Behörde für ihr Anliegen finden können.
Vertreten waren Studierende der Hochschulen Bochum, Mainz und Oldenburg sowie der Universitäten Tübingen, Augsburg, Freiburg und Heidelberg. Auch das Azubi-Team der Berufsschule Cuno II Hagen stellte sich erfolgreich den Aufgaben.
Eröffnet wurde der Hackathon von Kanzler Jens Egler, der die Teams von Seiten der Hochschule Mainz herzlich willkommen hieß und den Stellenwert der Veranstaltung für die Studierenden unterstrich. Dr. Jörg Kurpjuhn, Abteilungsleiter im Ministerium für Wirtschaft, Tourismus, Energie und Klima Rheinland-Pfalz (MWTEK), begrüßte die Teilnehmenden im Namen des Ministeriums und der GDI-DE. Er gehörte der Jury an, die die Preisträger kürte. Neben dem MWTEK unterstützte auch die Hochschule Bochum die Veranstaltung. Daten und hilfreiche Tools steuerten das Bundesamt für Kartographie und Geodäsie (BKG), das Bundesministerium für Digitales und Staatsmodernisierung (BMDS), die DB MindBox sowie das Start-Up Tobey GIS Consulting bei.
Die Studierenden zeigten sich begeistert darüber, mit tagesaktuellen Themen und berufsbezogenen Challenges arbeiten zu können. Besonders überzeugte sie die Möglichkeit, anwendungsnahe Use Cases zu entwickeln, die beispielsweise Behörden dabei unterstützen, präventiv tätig zu werden. Auch Organisation und Ablauf der Veranstaltung kamen sehr gut an.
Die hohe Qualität der Lösungsansätze für die bearbeiteten Challenges begeisterte die Jury — und machte ihr die Auswahl der ausgezeichneten Projekte der Studierenden-Teams nicht leicht. „Ich war im Vorfeld des Hackathons sehr gespannt, wie die zum Teil ja noch sehr jungen Teams mit den herausfordernden Challenges umgehen würden. Umso mehr freue ich mich, nun so funktionelle und kreative Lösungen zu sehen.“ stellte dann auch Dr. Jörg Kurpjuhn begeistert fest.
"Es freut uns sehr, dass wir den Hackathon bereits zum dritten Mal an der Hochschule Mainz ausrichten konnten und unsere Einladung auf große Resonanz gestoßen ist“, erklärte Prof. Dr. Markus Schaffert, Professor an der Hochschule Mainz und ebenfalls Jury-Mitglied. "Die studentischen Teams haben sich in kurzer Zeit in komplexe Fragestellungen eingearbeitet, eigenständige Lösungsansätze entwickelt und diese technisch überzeugend umgesetzt“.
Nun geht es für das Team der Koordinierungsstelle GDI-DE darum, die siegreichen Entwürfe so aufzubereiten, dass sie Interessierten in Kürze auf der Webseite präsentiert werden können. So soll die Möglichkeit geschaffen werden, die Nachnutzung und den tatsächlichen Einsatz der Lösungen zu unterstützen.
